author: Francis Dennig

abstract: |
  PLACEHOLDER — draft for discussion, to be tightened once the results are final.
  Hard-currency debt against local-currency revenue is priced as though the whole
  nominal exchange rate were at risk. Where the power purchase agreement indexes
  the tariff to domestic prices, it is not: inflation passes through to the dollar
  value of revenue, and only the residual movement is left uncovered. We measure
  that residual directly as the dollar unit-revenue index $X = P/S$, and price
  cover on it actuarially over every rolling 15-year window of African WDI data
  since 1995. The instrument — an emergency liquidity facility that advances debt
  service whenever $X$ sits below its level at financial close, is repaid out of
  later surpluses, and settles net at maturity — costs about 30 basis points on
  the loan margin pooled across countries, and about 165 basis points for
  Nigeria. The affordability comes from the cyclicality of the
  residual, not from optimism about depreciation: an institution with long-term
  capital, able to hold a position through a 5-10 year adverse swing, bears
  materially less risk than the market prices.

```{python}
# compute_V, shading helpers, and the two-axis country_chart).
import numpy as np
import altair as alt
# Render charts to static PNG in the kernel (needs vl-convert-python, installed
# in .venv). Viewer-proof: notebook front-ends (VS Code / JupyterLab) render raw
# vegalite JSON through their own vega bundle and can inject a dark display
# theme that overrides the spec config, hiding axis/legend/title text. PNGs
# also carry straight through to Quarto PDF. For interactive tooltips while
# exploring, temporarily switch to: alt.renderers.enable('html')
alt.renderers.enable('png', scale_factor=2.0)

# Theme pinning ALL ink colors, not just the background: dark-mode viewers
# (VS Code / JupyterLab) render vega-lite with the dark theme's light text,
# so forcing only a white background yields invisible axis labels, ticks and
# legends (white-on-white). alt.theme is the non-deprecated 5.5+ API.
@alt.theme.register('paper', enable=True)
def _paper_theme():
    ink = '#333333'
    return {'config': {
        'background': 'white',
        'title': {'color': ink},
        'axis': {'labelColor': ink, 'titleColor': ink, 'tickColor': ink,
                 'domainColor': ink, 'gridColor': '#dddddd'},
        'legend': {'labelColor': ink, 'titleColor': ink},
        'header': {'labelColor': ink, 'titleColor': ink},
        'text': {'color': ink},
    }}

def compute_V(cdata, t0, T, col='X', rho=discount_rate, n=window_length):
    """Net cover balance V over [t0, T], where t0 is the year of financial close
    and T is maturity. The close-year observation sets the strike and is not a
    fixing, so the T - t0 fixings run t0+1..T and are discounted at elapsed
    years 1..T-t0. Normalised by the annuity factor A_{n,rho} so that it reads
    as a fraction of the debt stock (D = A_{n,rho} * annual debt service)."""
    win = cdata[(cdata['year'] >= t0) & (cdata['year'] <= T)].sort_values('year')
    v = win[col].to_numpy()
    g = v[1:] / v[0] - 1.0
    t = np.arange(1, len(g) + 1, dtype=float)
    dfactors = (1.0 + rho) ** (-t)
    af = (1.0 - (1.0 + rho) ** -n) / rho
    return float(np.sum(g * dfactors) / af)

def _shade_and_text_layers(cdata, col, hline, shades):
    layers = []
    text_rows = []
    if shades and hline is not None:
        for shade in shades:
            y_start, y_end, color = shade[0], shade[1], shade[2]
            label = shade[3] if len(shade) > 3 else None
            seg = cdata[(cdata['year'] >= y_start) & (cdata['year'] <= y_end)].copy()
            seg['hline'] = hline
            layers.append(
                alt.Chart(seg).mark_area(opacity=0.3, color=color).encode(
                    x=alt.X('year:O'),
                    y=alt.Y(f'{col}:Q'),
                    y2=alt.Y2('hline:Q')
                )
            )
            if label is not None and not seg.empty:
                mid_year = int(seg['year'].iloc[len(seg)//2])
                mid_y = (seg[col].mean() + hline) / 2
                text_rows.append({'year': mid_year, 'y': mid_y, 'text': label, 'color': color})
    return layers, text_rows

def country_chart(iso3, start_year=start_year,
                  x_hline=None, shades=None,
                  usd_hline=None, usd_shades=None,
                  usd_y_range=None, h_y_range=None,
                  price_base_year=None):

    country_name = cdata['country'].iloc[0]

    # Optional third series: the price level, normalised to 1 in the base year.
    # It shares the left-hand axis with X because both are indices and
    # X = P * (1/S) - the point being that X's path is P's smooth climb times
    # the nominal rate's fall. Vega-Lite can only place two y-axes.
    p_label = None
    if price_base_year is not None:
        p_base = df[(df['iso3'] == iso3) & (df['year'] == price_base_year)]['cpi'].iloc[0]
        cdata['P_idx'] = cdata['cpi'] / p_base
        p_label = f'P ({price_base_year}=1)'

    legend_setting = alt.Legend(title="Series", orient="bottom")
    # Pinned series colours, in legend order: X, P, 1/S. The legend follows the
    # scale domain, and pinning also stops a third domain value from re-sorting
    # the domain and recolouring X and 1/S in the panels that show P.
    series_scale = alt.Scale(
        domain=['X'] + ([p_label] if p_label else []) + ['1/S'],
        range=['#4c78a8'] + (['#54a24b'] if p_label else []) + ['#f58518'],
    )

    usd_scale = alt.Scale(domain=list(usd_y_range)) if usd_y_range is not None else alt.Undefined
    x_scale = alt.Scale(domain=list(h_y_range)) if h_y_range is not None else alt.Undefined

    # --- RIGHT AXIS: 1/S ---
    # Drawn first so the X/P group layers on top of the 1/S shading; the axis
    # side is set by the explicit orient, not by layer order.
    usd_layers = []
    usd_shade_layers, usd_text_rows = _shade_and_text_layers(cdata, 'usd_per_lcu', usd_hline, usd_shades)
    usd_layers.extend(usd_shade_layers)

    usd_layers.append(
        alt.Chart(cdata).mark_line(point=True).encode(
            x=alt.X('year:O', title='Year'),
            y=alt.Y('usd_per_lcu:Q', title='1/S  (USD per LCU)',
                    axis=alt.Axis(orient='right'), scale=usd_scale),
            color=alt.Color('Metric:N', scale=series_scale, legend=legend_setting),
            tooltip=['year', 'usd_per_lcu']
        ).transform_calculate(Metric="'1/S'")
    )

    if usd_hline is not None:
        usd_layers.append(
            alt.Chart(pd.DataFrame({'y':[usd_hline]})).mark_rule(color='blue', strokeDash=[4,4]).encode(
                y=alt.Y('y:Q')
            )
        )

    if usd_text_rows:
        usd_layers.append(
            alt.Chart(pd.DataFrame(usd_text_rows)).mark_text(fontSize=14, fontWeight='bold').encode(
                x=alt.X('year:O'),
                y=alt.Y('y:Q'),

                color=alt.Color('color:N', scale=None, legend=None)
            )
        )

    usd_chart = alt.layer(*usd_layers)

    # --- LEFT AXIS: X, and P when requested ---
    x_axis_title = ('X = P / S  (USD per local basket)' if p_label is None
                    else f'X = P / S  (USD per local basket), and P ({price_base_year}=1)')
    x_layers = []
    x_shade_layers, x_text_rows = _shade_and_text_layers(cdata, 'X', x_hline, shades)
    x_layers.extend(x_shade_layers)

    x_layers.append(
        alt.Chart(cdata).mark_line(point=True).encode(
            x=alt.X('year:O', title='Year'),
            y=alt.Y('X:Q', title=x_axis_title, axis=alt.Axis(orient='left'), scale=x_scale),
            color=alt.Color('Metric:N', scale=series_scale, legend=legend_setting),

        ).transform_calculate(Metric="'X'")
    )

    if x_hline is not None:
        x_layers.append(
            alt.Chart(pd.DataFrame({'y':[x_hline]})).mark_rule(color='red', strokeDash=[4,4]).encode(
                y=alt.Y('y:Q')
            )
        )

    if x_text_rows:
        x_layers.append(
            alt.Chart(pd.DataFrame(x_text_rows)).mark_text(fontSize=14, fontWeight='bold').encode(
                x=alt.X('year:O'),
                y=alt.Y('y:Q'),
                text=alt.Text('text:N'),
                color=alt.Color('color:N', scale=None, legend=None)
            )
        )

    if p_label is not None:
        x_layers.append(
            alt.Chart(cdata).mark_line(point=True).encode(
                x=alt.X('year:O', title='Year'),
                # Same axis spec as the X layer: the two specs merge into the
                # single left-hand axis, whose domain unions both series.
                # (axis=None here instead suppresses that merged axis.)
                y=alt.Y('P_idx:Q', title=x_axis_title,
                        axis=alt.Axis(orient='left'), scale=x_scale),

    x_chart = alt.layer(*x_layers)

    return alt.layer(usd_chart, x_chart).resolve_scale(y='independent').properties(
        title=f"{country_name} (from {start_year})",

dza_data = df[(df['iso3']=='DZA') & (df['year']>=start_year)].dropna(subset=['X'])
```

```{python}
#| include: false
#| execution: {iopub.execute_input: '2026-09-17T07:26:23.868720Z', iopub.status.busy: '2026-09-17T07:26:23.868720Z', iopub.status.idle: '2026-09-17T07:26:24.420641Z', shell.execute_reply: '2026-09-17T07:26:24.420641Z'}
# Ported from wdi_hybrid_analysis.ipynb, cell 3.
def compute_terminal_residuals_wdi(
    df,
    years=window_length,
    discount_rate=discount_rate,
    window_mode="rolling", # or "two_non_overlapping",  # 
    col="X",
    start_year=None,
):
    """Mirror of source.data_analysis_functions.compute_terminal_residuals,
    operating directly on the wdi_africa_long-shaped df with columns:
    iso3, country, year, exchange_rate, cpi, us_cpi, usd_per_lcu, X, Q.

    `years` is the tenor n: the number of debt-service payments, and equally the
    number of live fixings. A window therefore spans n+1 annual observations,
    from financial close at window_start through maturity at window_end =
    window_start + n. The close-year observation sets the strike (R = 0 there by
    construction, since the debt is sized to close-year cash flow) and is NOT a
    fixing -- including it would park A^-1 (1+rho)^-1 ~ 9% of the averaging
    weight on a return that cannot move, and make the first debt-service year
    riskless by assumption.

    For each country, slides the window over the series in `col`, computes
    R_it = v/v[window_start] - 1 at the n fixings, discounts them back to close
    at elapsed years 1..n, and returns the net cover balance V: the present
    value of lifetime P&L (V_raw) normalised by the annuity factor A into a
    fraction of the debt stock.
    If `start_year` is given, df is filtered to year >= start_year before
    any windowing.
    """
    if start_year is not None:
        df = df[df["year"] >= start_year]

    af = (1 - (1 + discount_rate) ** -years) / discount_rate
    n_obs = years + 1           # close-year observation, then n fixings
    out = []

    for iso3, g in df.dropna(subset=[col]).groupby("iso3"):
        g = g.sort_values("year").reset_index(drop=True)
        n = len(g)
        if n < n_obs:
            continue

        if window_mode == "two_non_overlapping":
            # Consecutive tenors share an endpoint -- the maturity of the first
            # is the close of the second -- so the step is n, not n+1.
            starts = list(range(0, n - n_obs + 1, years))[:2]
        elif window_mode == "rolling":
            starts = list(range(0, n - n_obs + 1))
        else:
            raise ValueError("window_mode must be 'two_non_overlapping' or 'rolling'")

        for i0 in starts:
            win = g.iloc[i0:i0 + n_obs]
            if win[col].isna().any():
                continue

            base = float(win[col].iloc[0])
            R_it = (win[col].to_numpy()[1:] / base) - 1.0
            t = np.arange(1, years + 1, dtype=float)
            dfactors = (1.0 + discount_rate) ** (-t)

            V_raw = float(np.sum(R_it * dfactors))
            V = V_raw / af
            loss = min(V, 0.0)

            out.append({
                "iso3": iso3,
                "country": win["country"].iloc[0],
                "window_start": int(win["year"].iloc[0]),
                "window_end": int(win["year"].iloc[-1]),
                "baseline": base,
                "V": V,
                "loss": loss,
            })

    return pd.DataFrame(out)


from scipy.optimize import brentq


def equivalent_rate(expected_loss, discount_rate, years=15):
    """Translate an expected PV loss (fraction of debt stock) into the
    equivalent interest rate.

    The expected loss is treated as additional debt, so the inflated principal
    is (1 + |expected_loss|). Solve for the rate r_new at which the annuity on
    the original principal (=1) equals the annuity on the inflated principal
    priced at the original rate, i.e.
        af(r_new, years) == af0 / (1 + |loss|),
    where `af0` is the original annuity factor. af is strictly decreasing in r,
    so the root is unique.
    """
    af0 = (1 - (1 + discount_rate) ** -years) / discount_rate
    target_af = af0 / (1.0 + abs(expected_loss))
    af = lambda r: (1.0 - (1.0 + r) ** -years) / r
    return brentq(lambda r: af(r) - target_af, 1e-9, 1.0)
```

# Motivation: the currency mismatch that blocks the deal

Currency mismatch between local currency revenues in developing countries and the cost of hard currency debt service holds up many infrastructure finance transactions. When such hard currency credit has been provided for developing country electricity generation infrastructure, the currency risk has often been placed on the national utility - "offtaker" - through dollarised power purchase agreements (PPAs). This has led to an exacerbation of these utilities' financial woes from currency devaluations. This has had the knock-on effect of increasing offtaker risk for such projects and generating an additional impediment to the financing of electricity generation projects. Capital costs for such projects are thus affected two-fold by the currency mismatch, by the direct currency risk and by the induced offtaker risk.

This analysis suggests that, when inflation is borne by the consumer, the residual - real - currency risk, is limited when borne by an institution with sufficiently long term capital. This is due to the relatively long period in the cyclicality of the real exchange rate. An institution exposed to real exchange rate risk and able to weather adverse movements lasting 5-10 years will bear significantly less risk than is commonly assumed, even for developing country currency risk. As a result, such institutions are well placed to offer affordable cover to such transactions.

This proposal, analogous to the emergency liquidity facility of the EcoInvest Brazil platform provided by the IaDB, provides insurance against shortfalls in hard currency debt service *triggered by adverse movements the exchange and inflation rates*. The pre-requisite for cover is that revenues are indexed to local currency inflation through appropriate clauses in the power purchase agreement. As we show below, this strips inflation out of the nominal exchange rate risk, leaving only a real exchange rate risk component, which is bounded and cyclical, and consequently allows for affordable cover.

## Notation

**Parameters, fixed throughout:** tenor $n=15$; nominal discount rate $\rho$ = `{python} f"{discount_rate:.2f}"`; annuity factor $A_{n,\rho}=\sum_{k=1}^{n}(1+\rho)^{-k}=\dfrac{1-(1+\rho)^{-n}}{\rho}$ (the index $k$ counts elapsed years).

**Unit of observation:** a *window* $w=(i,\underline{t})\in\mathcal{W}$ — country $i$, financial close at $\underline{t}$, maturity $\bar{t}\equiv\underline{t}+n$. The pool has $N=|\mathcal{W}|$ windows. Windows share the common length $n$ but start at different dates, so calendar years are indexed absolutely, $t=\underline{t},\dots,\bar{t}$, and a window sum runs $\sum_{t=\underline{t}+1}^{\bar{t}}$; the elapsed year $t-\underline{t}$ carries the discounting, so windows of equal length are discounted identically wherever they sit in the sample.

- $P_{i,t}$ — domestic price level (CPI), in LCU; $p\equiv\ln P$, inflation $\pi=\dot p$
- $P^{*}_{t}$ — US price level; $\pi^{*}$ — US inflation
- $S_{i,t}$ — nominal exchange rate in LCU per USD, so $\dot s>0$ is a depreciation of the local currency; $s\equiv\ln S$
- $X_{i,t}\equiv P_{i,t}/S_{i,t}$ — the **dollar unit-revenue index**: the nominal USD value of a fixed domestic basket, i.e. what a kWh of inflation-indexed local revenue is worth in dollars. $x\equiv\ln X=p-s$, so $\dot x=\pi-\dot s$. It is *not* the real exchange rate — it is deflated by domestic prices only
- $Q_{i,t}\equiv X_{i,t}/P^{*}_{t}$ — the real exchange rate, $X$ deflated a second time by the US price level. Used in the pricing decomposition only
- $R_{w,t}\equiv X_{i,t}/X_{i,\underline{t}}-1$, for $t=\underline{t},\dots,\bar{t}$ — cumulative (holding-period) return on $X$ since financial close, so $R_{w,\underline{t}}=0$
- $\tau,\ c,\ \bar{E}$ — real tariff, real unit cost, constant energy output
- $r$ — loan interest rate; $\rho$ — discount rate; we set $r=\rho$ throughout
- $A_{n,\rho}$ — annuity factor: the present value of a unit annuity over $n$ periods at rate $\rho$
- $D$ — debt stock; $\bar\delta$ — level annual debt service, with $D=A_{n,\rho}\,\bar\delta$
- $\Lambda_w\equiv\bar\delta\sum_{t=\underline{t}+1}^{\bar{t}}R_{w,t}(1+\rho)^{-(t-\underline{t})}$ — discounted loan-life P&L
- $V_w\equiv\dfrac{\Lambda_w}{D}=\dfrac{1}{A_{n,\rho}}\displaystyle\sum_{t=\underline{t}+1}^{\bar{t}}\frac{R_{w,t}}{(1+\rho)^{t-\underline{t}}}$ — the **net cover balance**: the terminal balance of the cover account as a fraction of principal
- $L_w\equiv D\max(-V_w,0)$ — ultimate net loss to the Facility
- $\Psi$ — level annual premium as a share of debt service; $\Delta r$ — margin-equivalent interest-rate add-on
- $\mathbb{E}[\cdot]$ — expectation; $\mathbb{E}_N[\cdot]\equiv N^{-1}\sum_{w\in\mathcal{W}}[\cdot]$ — sample mean over the pool

In the code below, the DataFrame column `X` holds $X_{i,t}$ (computed as `cpi / exchange_rate`), `Q` holds $Q_{i,t}$ (`X / us_cpi`), and `exchange_rate` holds $S_{i,t}$.

## A stylised project

The analysis below focuses on $X_{i,t}=P_{i,t}/S_{i,t}$, where $P_i$ is the domestic price level and $S_i$ the nominal exchange rate in LCU per USD. As an index, $X$ measures the change in the USD value of a fixed local basket of goods. If the local price of electricity is made to grow at the national inflation rate, $X$ also measures the evolution of the USD value of a MWh. It is easy to see (and we show in detail below) that when tariffs are inflation-adjusted, $X$ is a good measure of the dollar cash flows available for debt service.

Consider, for simplicity, a project in country $i$ reaching financial close at $\underline{t}$ — a window $w=(i,\underline{t})$ — and generating a constant amount of energy $\bar{E}$ over the $n$ years of its debt service, at constant real unit cost $c$, excluding hard-currency debt service, and selling at an inflation-indexed real tariff $\tau$. Debt service runs over the calendar years $t=\underline{t},\underline{t}+1,\dots,\bar{t}$, where $\bar{t}\equiv\underline{t}+n$ is maturity. We keep the calendar year as the index, rather than counting from one, because the empirical work below runs the same $n$-year window from every possible start date: the window's identity lives in its limits $\underline{t}$ and $\bar{t}$, while the elapsed year $t-\underline{t}$ does the discounting. Nominal local-currency revenue is $P_{i,t}\,\tau\,\bar{E}$ and earnings before debt service are $P_{i,t}(\tau-c)\bar{E}$. That is, local-currency cash flows available for debt service (CFADS) are a constant growing at the rate of inflation, and CFADS in dollars are

$$
\text{CF}^{\$}_{w,t} \;=\; X_{i,t}\,(\tau-c)\,\bar{E},
\qquad t=\underline{t},\dots,\bar{t} .
$$

For the sake of exposition, we consider a stylised project in which all debt is in hard currency and debt service is a constant $\bar\delta$ dollars over the entire repayment period.

The annuity factor, for which the formula below pops out of the finite geometric sum, is defined as the present value of a 1 unit annuity for $n$ years at a discount rate of $\rho$, with $k$ counting elapsed years:
$$
A_{n,\rho}=\sum_{k=1}^{n}(1+\rho)^{-k}=\frac{1-(1+\rho)^{-n}}{\rho}
$$

By that definition, the principal that is borrowed at an interest rate $r=\rho$ and repaid with a constant annuity $\bar\delta$ over $n$ years is simply
$$
D = A_{n,\rho} \cdot \bar\delta
$$

We will assume that the debt has been sized so that annual debt service is exactly equal to the dollar CFADS in the first year of operations (and of debt service): $\text{CF}^{\$}_{w,\underline{t}} = X_{i,\underline{t}}(\tau-c)\bar{E} \equiv \bar\delta = D/A_{n,\rho}$

This automatically results in a debt service coverage ratio (DSCR) of one at close, leaving zero buffer for future FX swings; dollar debt service is constant by assumption and CFADS only just cover the debt service requirement when $X_{i,t} = X_{i,\underline{t}}$ is constant. The assumption also implies zero profit in the constant $X$ scenario, a debt service shortfall (and technical default) when $X$ decreases and a surplus when $X$ increases.

Project finance structures usually require a DSCR greater than 120% as a buffer against various risks to which the cash flows are exposed. Still, our assumption of zero buffer is without loss of generality, since the main affordability result below is only strengthened if projected $\text{DSCR}_t>1$.


Mathematically the PnL (surplus or shortfall) in year $t$ due to currency or price movements is
$$
\text{PL}_{w,t} = \text{CF}^{\$}_{w,t} - \bar\delta = \bar\delta \frac{\text{CF}^{\$}_{w,t} - \text{CF}^{\$}_{w,\underline{t}}}{\text{CF}^{\$}_{w,\underline{t}}} = \bar\delta \cdot  R_{w,t}
$$
where
$$
R_{w,t} \;\equiv\; \frac{\text{CF}^{\$}_{w,t}}{\text{CF}^{\$}_{w,\underline{t}}} - 1 \;=\; \frac{X_{i,t}}{X_{i,\underline{t}}} - 1 ,
\qquad t=\underline{t},\dots,\bar{t}
$$

is the cumulative return on $X$ since close — a holding-period return, not a per-period flow — and $R_{w,\underline{t}}=0$ by construction, since the debt is sized to the close-year cash flow.

Given a discount rate $\rho$, the present value at financial close of the loan life P&L is

$$
\Lambda_w \;=\; \sum_{t=\underline{t}+1}^{\bar{t}}\bar\delta\, \frac{R_{w,t}}{(1+\rho)^{t-\underline{t}}} = D \cdot \underbrace{\frac{1}{A_{n,\rho}}\sum_{t=\underline{t}+1}^{\bar{t}} \frac{R_{w,t}}{(1+\rho)^{t-\underline{t}}}}_{V_w}
$$
Through the constant debt service assumption we can calculate the profit as $V_w$ times the total debt stock. Time varying repayment profiles reweight the sum but don't have a material impact on the results as we show in the robustness checks below.

As such the main object of interest is the *net cover balance*
$$
V_w \;=\; \frac{\Lambda_w}{D} = \frac{1}{A_{n,\rho}} \sum_{t=\underline{t}+1}^{\bar{t}} \frac{1}{(1+\rho)^{t-\underline{t}}} \frac{X_{i,t}- X_{i,\underline{t}}}{X_{i,\underline{t}}}
$$

Two windows of the same country with different closes therefore differ only in the limits of this sum and in the level $X_{i,\underline{t}}$ against which the path is measured: the discount weights $(1+\rho)^{-(t-\underline{t})}$ are the same $n$ numbers for every window. That is what makes the pooled average over $\mathcal{W}$ below a comparison of like with like.

## Inflation and the exchange rate

Consider the case of the Algerian Dinar to understand how the exchange rate and price level affect the macroeconomic exposure of a project with local currency revenues. The figure plots $X_{i,t} = P_{i,t}/S_{i,t}$ for the 30 year period between 1995 and 2024, along with its components: the price level $P_{i,t}$ and the nominal exchange rate $1/S_{i,t}$ (in USD per LCU). In the plotted representation the growth rates of the components sum up visually to the growth rate of $X$.

Consider the macroeconomic movements that a local currency project reaching financial close in 1998 and paying 15 years of hard currency debt service must contend with.

During that period the nominal exchange rate dropped 26% from 1.7 to 1.3 Dollar cents per Dinar, with the bulk of the depreciation (22%) taking place in the first two years. 

If the project had (admittedly unlikely) constant nominal Dinar cashflows, it would have had lower dollar CFADS than at financial close in every single year of its debt service (the orange path for $1/S_{i,t}$). Unhedged a constant Dinar cashflow would have been worth only 88% of its 1998 dollar value in 1999 and only 78% in 2000. If such a project had constant USD debt service commitments valued at 100% of the 1998 dollar value for the 15 years from 1998 to 2013, the depreciation would result in an inability to fully service the debt, amounting to a total shortfall of 20% of the original principal (in present value terms at financial close), or two years worth of debt service.

Looking instead at $X_{i,t}$, we see that a project with inflation adjusted cashflows in Dinar would have also been in the red between 1998 and 2006, when the dollar value of its revenue stayed below the level at which the debt was sized. Discounted back to financial close, that run of shortfalls is worth 7% of the debt stock: the red area in the chart. Between 2002 and 2013, however, inflation outpaced depreciation and $X_{i,t}$ recovered, so that from 2006 onwards the project ran a surplus worth 11% of the debt stock: the green area.

While the green area is greater than the red area, from the point of view of the project the later gain is discounted more than the earlier loss. At the 5% discount rate used in the calculation the 11% gain is actually closer to a 7% gain in present value terms comparable to the loss, so that the gain almost exactly compensates for the shortfall. The cumulative currency and price movements had no overall impact on the project's ability to service its debt.

The depreciation episode is one of liquidity rather than solvency. 


## Solvency and liquidity

As the example of Algeria illustrates, for a project with inflation indexed local currency revenue and and hard currency debt service, the risk implied by the currency mismatch has two components: it is a long position on local inflation and a short position on appreciation of the dollar. In the example inflation eventually comes in to compensate of an appreciation of the dollar. Macroeconomic theory predicts such compensatory movements over time and, as we shall see below, this is what happens more often than not in the historical macroeconomic series in Africa.

The eventual rebalancing of $X$ through the inflation-exchange-rate dynamics ensures the long run solvency of a Dinar project in the 1998-2013 sample. However, such a project would still run into liquidity issues quite soon, as illustrated by the red area in the chart. Unless lender and borrower had accounted for a DSCR in excess of 150% along with a significant reserve account, standard debt covenants would put such a project into technical default by the 4th or 5th year of debt service. 

An emergency liquidity line to the borrower in hard currency could avert such a technical default and the consequent refinancing. Provided sufficient certainty in the eventual rebalancing of $X$ ensuring solvency of the debtor, such an emergency liquidity line can be provided quite cheaply by an entity with sufficiently patient capital (and solvency buffer). The proposal below does just that.

## The emergency liquidity facility

Let the **Facility** offer cover that, in return for an annual premium, supplies emergency liquidity to a project with hard currency debt when the currency moves against it. In the insurance register the Facility is the underwriter and the project the insured; in the finance register the Facility is a protection seller and the project the beneficiary, and an obligor once it has drawn. The cover has two legs, and keeping them apart is what makes it priceable:

- a **liquidity leg** --- gross, reversible, paid out during the tenor, and carrying no loss content of its own;
- a **risk leg** --- net, terminal, and where the loss actually lives.

Recall that $w=(i,\underline{t})$ and $R_{w,t} = \frac{X_{i,t}}{X_{i,\underline{t}}} - 1$, and consider again a project with inflation indexed local currency revenues, constant hard currency debt service and $DSCR_t = 1$ for the entire repayment period.

**The liquidity leg.** The condition $R_{w,t}<0$ is the **drawing trigger**: whenever a devaluation puts the dollar value of revenue below its level at financial close, the Facility **advances** $\bar\delta \cdot|R_{w,t}|$ and the project meets its debt service in full. The trigger is a currency movement and not a default --- nothing in the structure is a credit event, and the lender continues to see a performing loan. Whenever $R_{w,t}>0$, the project pays the surplus into an interest-bearing USD **experience account**: a pledged reserve, in the finance register, whose running balance stands against the drawings outstanding.

Recalling the Algerian currency and price movements, the Facility would have made drawings worth 7% of the original loan between 1998 and 2006, and the experience account would have taken in 11% between 2006 and 2013 (the red and green areas in the chart, each valued at the start of its own segment).

**The risk leg.** At maturity $\bar{t}$ the position is **commuted**: the two sides settle net once and all obligations are extinguished. A positive experience account balance is returned to the project; a negative one --- drawings that the later surpluses did not repay --- is borne by the Facility. Drawings are therefore repayable solely out of subsequent favourable movements: limited recourse during the tenor, non-recourse at maturity. The balance in the experience account is the project's money throughout, which is what makes this cover an option rather than a swap --- the project keeps its upside and the Facility is left with the downside alone.

**Equivalently, an Asian put.** The structure of the risk has an exact counterpart in derivatives. What the Facility owes at commutation turns not on where $X$ ends up but on its average level over the tenor, $\bar{X}_{w}$, and it owes anything at all only if that average falls short of the level at financial close:
$$
\text{payoff} \;=\; \frac{D}{X_{i,\underline{t}}}\,\max\big(X_{i,\underline{t}}-\bar{X}_{w},\,0\big) .
$$
That is the payoff of an arithmetic average-rate put --- an Asian put --- and the Facility is short it. The underlying is $X$, the dollar unit-revenue index. The strike is $X_{i,\underline{t}}$, its level at close, so the option is struck at the money spot, which is also the reference level for the facility. The fixings are the annual observations of $X$ over the tenor, the averaging weights are the discount factors, so that early years count for more than late ones, and the notional is the debt stock. The reading is useful because averaging is what makes Asian options cheap --- an average moves far less than the endpoint it averages over --- so cover written on the whole path costs materially less than cover on the terminal level of $X$ alone. Since we are working with a reverting series $X$, rather than a nominal exchange rate as is usually the case for Asian puts, the expected losses we compute below based on the realised historical distributions are significantly lower than what the derivative prices at.

Look at the path of $X$ in Nigeria to understand the loss profile of such cover.

In the graph below we trace all 15-year windows in the Nigerian data with a horizontal line starting at the value of $X$ at the window starting point.

Whenever $X$ is below a window's line, as it is between 1985 and 1993 for the window starting at 1985, a project servicing debt during that window is short of dollars and draws on the Facility. Whenever $X$ is above a window's line, as it is between 1993 and 1999 for the same window starting at 1985, the project runs a dollar surplus and pays into the experience account. The cumulative discounted area between the line and $X$ is the discounted loan life P&L over the 15-year window; normalised by the annuity factor, it is the net cover balance. If it is negative, the commutation leaves the Facility with a loss and we have drawn the horizontal line in red. If it is positive, no loss arises, the balance is commuted back to the project, and the horizontal line is painted in green.

The lines are drawn in increasingly darker shades, with a dot in the same shade painted on $X$ at the end of the 15-year window.

Underneath the time series, underneath the dot representing the end of the 15-year window, we plot $V_w$, the net cover balance, measured in present value terms at the beginning of the window.

Between 1985 and 2024 there are 25 15-year windows. Of those, 21 had a positive terminal value, ranging from 19% to 150% of the debt stock. Four windows, those immediately preceding the 1999 abandonment of the dollar peg and subsequent devaluation, had negative terminal values, the largest reaching 59% of the project debt stock.

```{python}
windows_chart_start = 1980


def _ramp(t, light, dark):
    """Hex color interpolated between `light` (t=0) and `dark` (t=1) in RGB."""
    lo = tuple(int(light[i:i + 2], 16) for i in (1, 3, 5))
    hi = tuple(int(dark[i:i + 2], 16) for i in (1, 3, 5))
    return '#%02x%02x%02x' % tuple(round(a + (b - a) * t) for a, b in zip(lo, hi))


def country_windows_styled(iso3, years=window_length, discount_rate=discount_rate,
                           step=1, first_start=windows_chart_start, ypad_frac=0.05):
    res = compute_terminal_residuals_wdi(
        df[df['iso3'] == iso3], years=years, discount_rate=discount_rate,
        window_mode="rolling", col="X", start_year=first_start).reset_index(drop=True)
    if step > 1:  # thin the rolling windows out if requested
        res = res[(res['window_start'] - res['window_start'].min()) % step == 0].reset_index(drop=True)

    g = (df[(df['iso3'] == iso3) & (df['year'] >= first_start)]
         .dropna(subset=['X']).sort_values('year'))
    country_name = g['country'].iloc[0]
    x0 = float(g['X'].iloc[0])
    base_year, last_year = int(g['year'].iloc[0]), int(g['year'].max())

    g = g.assign(idx=g['X'] / x0 * 100.0)            # index = 100 in the first year
    idx_by_year = dict(zip(g['year'], g['idx']))

    # bivariate color: hue = sign of residual (green gain / red loss); within each hue,
    # lightness ranks the window by start date (light = earliest of that colour -> dark =
    # latest). Normalising per colour (not over all windows) keeps the gradient visible even
    # when one colour has only a few, tightly-clustered windows (e.g. a handful of late losses).
    s = res['window_start']
    sign_pos = res['V'] >= 0

    def _shade(mask):
        sub = s[mask]
        if len(sub) == 0:
            return {}
        lo, sp = sub.min(), max(int(sub.max() - sub.min()), 1)
        return {int(ws): 0.25 + 0.6 * (ws - lo) / sp for ws in sub}

    gt, lt = _shade(sign_pos), _shade(~sign_pos)
    fills = [
        _ramp(gt[int(ws)], '#bae4b3', '#005a32') if resid >= 0
        else _ramp(lt[int(ws)], '#fcae91', '#a50f15')
        for ws, resid in zip(s, res['V'])
    ]

    wins = res.assign(
        residual=res['V'],
        start_idx=res['baseline'] / x0 * 100.0,
        end_idx=res['window_end'].map(idx_by_year),
        fill=fills)

    xscale = alt.Scale(domain=[base_year, last_year + 1])
    ypad = ypad_frac * (g['idx'].max() - g['idx'].min())
    yscale = alt.Scale(domain=[g['idx'].min() - ypad, g['idx'].max() + ypad],
                       zero=False, nice=False)
    year_vals = list(range(base_year, last_year + 1))
    fill_enc = alt.Color('fill:N', scale=None)
    tip = ['window_start', 'window_end', alt.Tooltip('residual:Q', format='+.4f')]

    # Layers share a scale per channel, so every layer must carry the SAME axis spec:
    # axis=None on any layer drops the guide, and differing fields with default titles make
    # Vega blank the title -- so define each axis once and reuse it everywhere.
    top_x = alt.Axis(values=year_vals, labels=False, ticks=True, title=None)  # ticks only
    top_y = alt.Axis(title=f'X index (=100 in {base_year})')
    bot_x = alt.Axis(values=year_vals, labelAngle=-60, format='d', title='year window ends')
    bot_y = alt.Axis(title='terminal residual / debt stock')

    # --- top panel: X index, window start-level markers + end dots (full-opacity so their
    #     gradient matches the residual bars below) ---
    ref100 = alt.Chart(pd.DataFrame({'y': [100]})).mark_rule(
        color='#bbb', strokeDash=[4, 4]).encode(y=alt.Y('y:Q', scale=yscale, axis=top_y))
    segs = alt.Chart(wins).mark_rule(strokeWidth=3).encode(
        x=alt.X('window_start:Q', scale=xscale, axis=top_x), x2='window_end:Q',
        y=alt.Y('start_idx:Q', scale=yscale, axis=top_y), color=fill_enc, tooltip=tip)
    hline = alt.Chart(g).mark_line(color='#222', strokeWidth=2).encode(
        x=alt.X('year:Q', scale=xscale, axis=top_x),
        y=alt.Y('idx:Q', scale=yscale, axis=top_y),
        tooltip=['year', alt.Tooltip('idx:Q', format='.1f')])
    dots = alt.Chart(wins).mark_point(filled=True, size=45).encode(
        x=alt.X('window_end:Q', scale=xscale, axis=top_x),
        y=alt.Y('end_idx:Q', scale=yscale, axis=top_y), color=fill_enc, tooltip=tip)
    top = (ref100 + segs + hline + dots).properties(
        width=550, height=300,
        title=alt.TitleParams(
            f"{country_name}: dollar unit-revenue index X (=100 in {base_year})",
            subtitle=["horizontal bar = each 15-yr window's start level, dot = where X ends;",
                      "green = gain, red = loss (darker = later window)"],
            anchor='start'))

    # --- bottom panel: terminal residual per window, at window end ---
    zero = alt.Chart(pd.DataFrame({'y': [0]})).mark_rule(color='#888').encode(
        y=alt.Y('y:Q', axis=bot_y))
    bars = alt.Chart(wins).mark_bar(width=10).encode(
        x=alt.X('window_end:Q', scale=xscale, axis=bot_x),
        y=alt.Y('residual:Q', axis=bot_y), color=fill_enc, tooltip=tip)
    bottom = (zero + bars).properties(width=550, height=160)

    return (alt.vconcat(top, bottom).resolve_scale(x='shared')
            .configure_view(strokeWidth=0)
            .configure_axis(grid=False, domainColor='#888', tickColor='#888'))


country_windows_styled('NGA')
```

## The actuarially fair premium

When $V_w \geq 0$ the experience account has repaid every drawing and the commutation returns the remainder to the project, so the Facility keeps nothing. Its loss on a window $w=(i,\underline{t})$ against debt $D$ --- the **ultimate net loss**, or terminal shortfall --- is the loan life P&L truncated at zero:
$$
L_w \;=\; D \cdot \max(-V_w,0)
$$
It can only be positive: the Facility absorbs the whole of every negative net cover balance (the 4 red windows in the Nigerian data) and takes nothing from the 21 positive ones.

The **pure premium** over a pool of windows $\mathcal{W}$ is the expected ultimate net loss over that pool,
$$
\mathbb{E}[L_w] = \mathbb{E}\big[D_w \cdot \max(-V_w,0)\big]
$$
Assuming that a similar amount of debt $D_w$ is covered in each window, it is estimated by the sample mean over the pool, with $N=\vert\mathcal{W}\vert$,
$$
\mathbb{E}_N[L_w] = \frac{D}{N}\sum_{w\in\mathcal{W}} \max(-V_w,0)
$$

The actuarially fair **level annual premium** --- the running fee the project pays for the cover --- is the annuity equivalent of that loss. Expressed as a fraction of the annuity paid as debt service, it is
$$
\Psi = \frac{\mathbb{E}_N[L_w]}{\bar\delta\cdot A_{n,\rho}} = \frac{D}{\bar\delta\cdot A_{n,\rho}} \frac{1}{N}\sum_{w\in\mathcal{W}} \max(-V_w,0) = \frac{1}{N}\sum_{w\in\mathcal{W}} \max(-V_w,0)
$$
The debt stock in the numerator cancels against annual debt service times the annuity factor in the denominator, so $\Psi$ is simply the average over the pool of the negative net cover balances, counting the positive ones as zero.

Going back up to the Nigerian data, and taking a simple average over the historical windows as an indication of future losses, the level annual premium is the sum of the 4 red bars divided by 25, the number of windows in the sample, which yields $\Psi = 6.9\%$. A Nigerian project buying cover priced off a purely Nigerian pool would pay 6.9% on top of each of its debt service payments.

## The equivalent interest rate spread

The pure premium is the natural quotation for an underwriter, but an investor prices a margin, and the same expected loss can be quoted differently.

level annual premium as a share of each debt service payment, $\Psi = 6.9\%$, is equally the present value of the expected ultimate net loss as a share of the principal --- dividing a present value by $\bar\delta A_{n,\rho}$ and dividing it by $D$ are the same operation.

By expressing annual payment as a share of the *original principal*, one gets a yearly quantity with a debt stock as the numerator:

$$
\frac{\Psi\,\bar\delta}{D} \;=\; \frac{\Psi}{A_{n,\rho}} \;=\; 0.67\% \text{ per year for Nigeria,}
$$

**but this is not the equivalent interest-rate spread, except on a bullet loan.**

On an annuity-amortising loan a margin accrues on the declining outstanding balance --- which averages just under 60% of the original principal over a 15-year tenor --- so the **spread**, or margin add-on, $\Delta r$ comes out about half as large again: 101bp for Nigeria against the 67bp above. It is computed exactly by treating the expected loss as additional principal and solving

$$
A_{n,\;\rho+\Delta r} \;=\; \frac{A_{n,\rho}}{1 + \Psi} .
$$

Underwriters quote the pure premium as a share of the covered exposure (debt service), and the margin-equivalent spread $\Delta r$ to investors. All three Nigerian figures here come from the 25-window sample opened in 1985 above

## The cost of cover for the whole African pool

The Nigerian pool is one country's worth of history. Widening $\mathcal{W}$ to every African country in the WDI panel gives $N = 1{,}055$ rolling 15-year windows across 50 countries, with financial close in every year from 1985 to 2009 (Lesotho excluded for uncorrected CPI basket breaks). Each window contributes one net cover balance $V_w$, the terminal balance of the cover account as a fraction of principal; @fig-pool-balance plots their distribution. Like the Nigerian figures above, this pool opens in 1985 and is not the 1995-start pool that the later sections of the draft use.

Two features of that distribution do the work.

First, **it is centred well to the right of zero**: $\mathbb{E}_N[V_w] = +0.22$ and the median window ends at $+0.18$. Over 15 years the typical African project's inflation-indexed dollar revenue does not merely keep up with its close-year level, it ends ahead of it by around a fifth of the debt stock in present value.

Second, **the left tail is thin but real**: 26% of windows end below zero, $\mathbb{E}_N[V_w \mid V_w<0] = -0.15$, and the worst single window in forty years of African data (Sudan, close 1991) ends at $-0.75$.

Applying the pricing formula of the previous section to this pool gives a level annual premium of

$$
\Psi \;=\; \mathbb{E}_N\big[\max(-V_w,0)\big] \;=\; \frac{1}{N}\sum_{w\in\mathcal{W}} \max(-V_w,0) \;=\; 4.0\% ,
$$

which is quoted on the three bases of the previous section as:

| Quote | Value | Read as |
|---|---|---|
| $\Psi$, share of each debt-service payment | **4.0%** | the underwriter's quote, and equally the PV of the expected ultimate net loss as a share of principal |
| $\Psi/A_{n,\rho}$, flat annual payment, share of original principal | **38 bp** | a fee on the face of the loan, correct only for a bullet |
| $\Delta r$, margin-equivalent spread | **58 bp** | the investor-facing number, on a 15-year annuity-amortising loan |

As in the Nigerian case, the spread exceeds the flat fee because a margin accrues on a balance that amortises to zero, averaging just under 60% of the original principal over the tenor.

**Where the affordability comes from.** Repricing the same 1,055 windows on the real exchange rate $Q_{i,t}=X_{i,t}/P^{*}_{t}$ instead of on $X$ gives $\Psi = 9.9\%$ and $\Delta r = 144$bp, with $\mathbb{E}_N[V_w] = +0.02$, a median of $-0.02$, and 53% of windows ending below zero. On the real rate alone, in other words, the cover is close to a fair bet: real appreciation and real depreciation are roughly equally likely over a 15-year horizon, which is the mean reversion the instrument relies on. The gap between 144bp and 58bp is the US price level. Since $X = Q\,P^{*}$ and $P^{*}$ rises about 45% over a 15-year window (2.5% a year), while the covered liability is *fixed in nominal dollars*, that drift accrues to the project. The cover is affordable for both reasons at once: the real rate mean-reverts within the tenor, and the debt service it protects does not index to anything.

**Liquidity is not solvency.** The gap between how often the Facility *lends* and how often it *loses* is the entire economics of the instrument. $X$ falls below its close-year level at some point in 67% of windows, and where it does it stays there for 6.9 of the 15 years on average. But only 26% of windows end with the cover account short. The Facility is, most of the time, a bridge that is repaid out of the later surplus, and it is priced on the residue rather than on the gross flow.

```{python}
#| include: false
#| execution: {iopub.execute_input: '2026-09-17T07:26:26.470034Z', iopub.status.busy: '2026-09-17T07:26:26.470034Z', iopub.status.idle: '2026-09-17T07:26:27.191270Z', shell.execute_reply: '2026-09-17T07:26:27.191270Z'}
# Pooled and country-level cost of cover.
#
# Same machinery as the Nigerian panel above, applied to every country rather
# than NGA alone: compute_terminal_residuals_wdi() over the whole frame, on X,
# with the window convention of @sec-method (n+1 observations, n fixings).
# Opens in 1985, like the Nigerian example, NOT at the global `start_year`
# (1995) that @sec-results and the indexation tables use -- hence the local
# names below, which must not collide with `residuals` / `by_country` there.
# `equivalent_rate` is the one defined in the setup cell at the top.
pool_start_year = 1985


def window_drawings(data, years=window_length, col="X", start_year=pool_start_year):
    """Per window: does the Facility ever advance, and in how many years?

    Counts fixings with R_{w,t} < 0, i.e. years in which the project falls short
    of its close-year dollar cash flow. This is the *liquidity* side of the
    instrument, as distinct from the terminal balance V_w, its *solvency* side.
    Windows are built exactly as in compute_terminal_residuals_wdi: n+1
    observations, of which the close year sets the strike and the n that follow
    are the fixings.
    """
    data = data[data["year"] >= start_year]
    n_obs = years + 1
    rows = []
    for iso3, g in data.dropna(subset=[col]).groupby("iso3"):
        g = g.sort_values("year").reset_index(drop=True)
        for i0 in range(0, len(g) - n_obs + 1):
            win = g.iloc[i0:i0 + n_obs]
            if win[col].isna().any():
                continue
            R_wt = win[col].to_numpy()[1:] / float(win[col].iloc[0]) - 1.0
            rows.append({"iso3": iso3, "window_start": int(win["year"].iloc[0]),
                         "any_draw": bool((R_wt < 0).any()),
                         "n_draw_years": int((R_wt < 0).sum()),
                         "worst_year": float(R_wt.min())})
    return pd.DataFrame(rows)


pool_res = compute_terminal_residuals_wdi(
    df, years=window_length, discount_rate=discount_rate,
    window_mode="rolling", col="X", start_year=pool_start_year)

psi_pool = -pool_res["loss"].mean()          # E_N[max(-V_w, 0)], share of debt service
psi_debt = psi_pool / annuity_factor         # flat annual payment, share of principal
dr_pool = equivalent_rate(psi_pool, discount_rate=discount_rate,
                          years=window_length) - discount_rate
p_loss = (pool_res["V"] < 0).mean()

worst = pool_res.loc[pool_res["V"].idxmin()]
print(f"Pool: N = {len(pool_res)} windows, {pool_res['iso3'].nunique()} countries, "
      f"closes {pool_res['window_start'].min()}-{pool_res['window_start'].max()}")
print(f"E_N[V] = {pool_res['V'].mean():+.4f}   median V = {pool_res['V'].median():+.4f}   "
      f"worst = {worst['V']:+.4f} ({worst['country']} {worst['window_start']}-{worst['window_end']})")
print(f"P(V < 0) = {p_loss:.3f}   E_N[V | V < 0] = {pool_res.loc[pool_res['V'] < 0, 'V'].mean():.4f}")
print(f"Psi = {psi_pool:.4f} of debt service;  Psi/A = {psi_debt * 1e4:.0f}bp of principal;  "
      f"delta_r = {dr_pool * 1e4:.0f}bp")

# Where the affordability comes from: the same windows priced on the real
# exchange rate Q = X / P*, which strips out the US price level. X is the
# priced object (the liability is nominal USD); Q isolates the real bet.
pool_res_q = compute_terminal_residuals_wdi(
    df, years=window_length, discount_rate=discount_rate,
    window_mode="rolling", col="Q", start_year=pool_start_year)
psi_pool_q = -pool_res_q["loss"].mean()
dr_pool_q = equivalent_rate(psi_pool_q, discount_rate=discount_rate,
                            years=window_length) - discount_rate
print(f"On Q instead of X: E_N[V] = {pool_res_q['V'].mean():+.4f}, "
      f"median {pool_res_q['V'].median():+.4f}, P(V<0) = {(pool_res_q['V'] < 0).mean():.3f}, "
      f"Psi = {psi_pool_q:.4f}, delta_r = {dr_pool_q * 1e4:.0f}bp")

# Liquidity side: how often, and for how long, the Facility is actually lending.
pool_draws = window_drawings(df)
print(f"windows with any drawing = {pool_draws['any_draw'].mean():.3f}; "
      f"drawing years = {pool_draws['n_draw_years'].mean():.1f} of {window_length} on average, "
      f"{pool_draws.loc[pool_draws['any_draw'], 'n_draw_years'].mean():.1f} among windows that draw")

# --- country by country, on three sample starts (the panels of @fig-country-spread).
# The premium is priced on each country's own windows; the later the start, the
# fewer windows per country (25 / 20 / 15) and the fewer crisis episodes in them.
panel_starts = (1985, 1990, 1995)


def country_spreads(start_year):
    """Country-level premium and margin-equivalent spread for one sample start.

    Carries the pool-level figures for that start along on every row, so a
    facet/panel can label itself without a second lookup.
    """
    res = compute_terminal_residuals_wdi(
        df, years=window_length, discount_rate=discount_rate,
        window_mode="rolling", col="X", start_year=start_year)
    bc = (res.groupby(["iso3", "country"], as_index=False)
             .agg(expected_loss=("loss", "mean"),
                  prob_loss=("V", lambda s: (s < 0).mean()),
                  mean_V=("V", "mean"),
                  n_windows=("V", "size")))
    bc["psi"] = -bc["expected_loss"]
    bc["psi_debt"] = bc["psi"] / annuity_factor
    bc["rate_increase"] = bc["psi"].apply(
        lambda p: equivalent_rate(p, discount_rate=discount_rate, years=window_length) - discount_rate)
    psi_p = -res["loss"].mean()
    bc["start"] = start_year
    bc["n_pool"] = len(res)
    bc["pooled"] = equivalent_rate(psi_p, discount_rate=discount_rate,
                                   years=window_length) - discount_rate
    return bc.sort_values("rate_increase", ascending=False).reset_index(drop=True)


spreads = pd.concat([country_spreads(y) for y in panel_starts], ignore_index=True)
pool_by_country = spreads[spreads["start"] == pool_start_year].reset_index(drop=True)

print()
print("sample-start sensitivity of the country spreads:")
for y in panel_starts:
    s = spreads[spreads["start"] == y]
    print(f"  from {y}: N = {int(s['n_pool'].iloc[0])} windows, {int(s['n_windows'].max())} per country; "
          f"pooled {s['pooled'].iloc[0] * 1e4:.0f}bp; country median {s['rate_increase'].median() * 1e4:.0f}bp, "
          f"mean {s['rate_increase'].mean() * 1e4:.0f}bp, max {s['rate_increase'].max() * 1e4:.0f}bp "
          f"({s.loc[s['rate_increase'].idxmax(), 'country']}); "
          f"{(s['psi'] == 0).sum()} at zero; {(s['rate_increase'] < 0.005).mean():.0%} below 50bp")

print()
print(f"country delta_r: median {pool_by_country['rate_increase'].median() * 1e4:.0f}bp, "
      f"mean {pool_by_country['rate_increase'].mean() * 1e4:.0f}bp, "
      f"pooled {dr_pool * 1e4:.0f}bp, "
      f"share below 50bp {(pool_by_country['rate_increase'] < 0.005).mean():.0%}")
print(f"{(pool_by_country['psi'] == 0).sum()} of {len(pool_by_country)} countries never end a "
      f"window in the red: {', '.join(pool_by_country.loc[pool_by_country['psi'] == 0, 'country'])}")
print(f"{(pool_by_country['n_windows'] == 25).sum()} countries have the full 25 windows")
print(pool_by_country[["country", "n_windows", "prob_loss", "mean_V", "psi", "rate_increase"]]
      .to_string(index=False,
                 formatters={"prob_loss": "{:.0%}".format, "mean_V": "{:+.3f}".format,
                             "psi": "{:.4f}".format, "rate_increase": "{:.4%}".format}))
```

## Country by country

Pooling is a pricing choice, not a fact about the risk. @fig-country-spread prices the same cover on each country's own windows and quotes the margin-equivalent spread $\Delta r$, the number an investor in that country would see. The top panel is the 1985 pool used above — 25 windows per country wherever the WDI series runs unbroken, fewer where it does not; the two below it repeat the exercise on samples opening in 1990 and 1995, with countries held in the 1985 order and the axes shared, so a column is one country priced on three samples.

Take the 1985 panel first. The dispersion is wide and the distribution is skewed. The median African country prices at **40bp** and 58% of countries sit below 50bp, but Libya (274bp), the Democratic Republic of Congo (189bp), Ethiopia (142bp), Algeria (142bp) and The Gambia (131bp) sit far out in the right tail. At the other end, eight countries — Egypt, Comoros, Guinea, Kenya, Liberia, Mauritius, Namibia and South Sudan — have no window since 1985 that ends below its close-year level at all, so their pure premium is exactly zero. Nigeria, the case traced above, prices at 101bp.

The lower panels show how much of that price is a statement about which episodes the sample contains. Moving the start to 1990 barely touches the pool (58bp to 55bp) but thins the middle of the distribution: the median country falls to 31bp and ten countries price at zero. Moving it to 1995 halves the pool to 30bp, takes the median country to 8bp, and leaves thirteen countries at zero — by then the sample has dropped the 1994 CFA devaluation and the worst of the Sudanese and Congolese episodes, and the cost is concentrated in a handful of names. What survives every cut is the shape: the same few countries stay in the tail — Libya prices between 274bp and 340bp on all three samples — while the majority of the continent prices in tens of basis points. The pooled number is the fragile part; the ranking is not.

The pooled 58bp is not a diversification gain over these country numbers. Expected loss is linear in the pool, so pooling can only *average*: the pooled figure differs from the unweighted country mean of 53bp merely because countries contribute unequal numbers of windows. What pooling buys sits on the capital side rather than the premium side — the variance of the Facility's aggregate outcome falls with the number of imperfectly correlated exposures, and that is what sizes the capital standing behind the promise, not its price.

A single pooled price is therefore a cross-subsidy from the Kenyas to the Libyas, and one that sponsors can see as clearly as the Facility can. That is an adverse-selection problem to be designed around — through risk-banded pricing, mandatory participation within a programme, or a deliberate decision to subsidise the tail — rather than an artefact to be averaged away. The policy discussion later in the draft returns to it.

## Tenor: what the horizon is worth {#sec-tenor}

Tenor and cover period are the same parameter in this design: the Facility is exposed from financial close to maturity, so $n$ fixes both how long the project is insured and how long the real exchange rate has to come back. If the affordability result rests on mean reversion inside the tenor, the premium should fall in $n$. @fig-tenor shows that it does — and that two quite different things are doing the work, which have to be separated before the figure means anything.

The first is the sample. With a fixed calendar window the closes run $\underline{t}=1985,\dots,2024-n$, so raising $n$ does not merely lengthen each window, it deletes the later close cohorts: at $n=25$ only the 1985–1999 closes survive, and those are the crisis-heavy vintages. A naive curve therefore moves the horizon and the set of projects at the same time. @fig-tenor controls for this with a **fixed cohort** — closes 1985–1999, the set available at every tenor on the grid, in the 43 countries whose series support $n=25$ — so that along the blue curve the horizon is the only thing that changes.

The second is the unit. $\Delta r$ is a margin on an amortising loan, so the same expected loss spread over more payments is a smaller margin whatever the risk is doing. The figure therefore quotes two of the premium's units at once — $\Psi$, the actuarial quote as a share of one debt-service payment, which carries no annuity, and the margin-equivalent $\Delta r$ — and adds $P(V_w<0)$, a frequency that carries no discounting at all. (The third quote, $\Psi/A$, tracks $\Delta r$ and is in the printed table.)

```{python}
#| include: false
#| execution: {iopub.execute_input: '2026-09-17T07:26:29.469680Z', iopub.status.busy: '2026-09-17T07:26:29.469680Z', iopub.status.idle: '2026-09-17T07:26:30.420997Z', shell.execute_reply: '2026-09-17T07:26:30.420354Z'}
# Tenor sensitivity (@fig-tenor): the same cover repriced at tenors from 5 to 25
# years on the 1985 pool, in the three units of @sec-instrument.
#
# Two samples per tenor, because a fixed calendar sample confounds the horizon
# with the close cohort: closes run pool_start_year .. 2024 - n, so raising n
# deletes the late vintages rather than only lengthening the windows. At n = 25
# only the 1985-1999 closes survive, and those are the crisis-heavy ones.
#   "all available windows" - every window at that tenor (the naive curve)
#   "fixed cohort"          - closes 1985-1999 only (the set available at every
#                             tenor in the grid), and only the countries whose
#                             series support n = 25, so that the horizon is the
#                             only thing moving along the curve.
tenor_grid = (5, 8, 10, 12, 15, 20, 25)
tenor_res = {n: compute_terminal_residuals_wdi(
                 df, years=n, discount_rate=discount_rate,
                 window_mode="rolling", col="X", start_year=pool_start_year)
             for n in tenor_grid}

cohort_last_close = int(df["year"].max()) - max(tenor_grid)
cohort_countries = sorted(tenor_res[max(tenor_grid)]["iso3"].unique())
cohort_label = f"fixed cohort: closes {pool_start_year}-{cohort_last_close}"

tenor_rows = []
for n in tenor_grid:
    a_n = (1 - (1 + discount_rate) ** -n) / discount_rate
    full = tenor_res[n]
    cohort = full[full["iso3"].isin(cohort_countries)
                  & (full["window_start"] <= cohort_last_close)]
    for label, res in [("all available windows", full), (cohort_label, cohort)]:
        psi = -res["loss"].mean()                       # share of one debt-service payment
        tenor_rows.append({
            "n": n,
            "sample": label,
            "psi_pct": 100 * psi,
            "psi_debt_bp": 1e4 * psi / a_n,             # flat annual payment, share of principal
            "dr_bp": 1e4 * (equivalent_rate(psi, discount_rate=discount_rate, years=n)
                            - discount_rate),
            "prob_loss": (res["V"] < 0).mean(),
            "n_windows": len(res),
            "n_countries": res["iso3"].nunique(),
        })

tenor = pd.DataFrame(tenor_rows)
print(f"Tenor sensitivity on the {pool_start_year} pool. Fixed cohort: closes "
      f"{pool_start_year}-{cohort_last_close} in the {len(cohort_countries)} countries "
      f"(of {tenor_res[window_length]['iso3'].nunique()}) whose series support n = {max(tenor_grid)}.")
print(tenor.to_string(index=False, formatters={
    "psi_pct": "{:.2f}%".format, "psi_debt_bp": "{:.0f}bp".format,
    "dr_bp": "{:.0f}bp".format, "prob_loss": "{:.0%}".format}))
```

```{python}
def tenor_panel(field, axis_title, fmt, show_x):
    """One stacked panel of @fig-tenor: the same two curves in a different unit.

    Every panel carries the same legend spec rather than suppressing it on two
    of the three: with the colour scale resolved as shared, Vega-Lite hoists one
    legend to the concat level, and a panel that disables it kills the hoisted
    legend for all of them.
    """
    x_axis = alt.Axis(values=list(tenor_grid), grid=False, labels=show_x, ticks=show_x,
                      title="n  (tenor, and equally the cover period, in years)" if show_x else None)
    line = alt.Chart(tenor).mark_line(point=True, strokeWidth=2).encode(
        x=alt.X("n:Q", scale=alt.Scale(domain=[4, 26]), axis=x_axis),
        y=alt.Y(f"{field}:Q", scale=alt.Scale(domainMin=0),
                axis=alt.Axis(format=fmt, title=axis_title, titleFontSize=10)),
        color=alt.Color("sample:N", scale=tenor_scale,
                        legend=alt.Legend(title=None, orient="bottom")),
        tooltip=tenor_tip)
    return (tenor_rule + line).properties(width=460, height=115)


alt.vconcat(
    tenor_panel("dr_bp", "Δr  (bp on the margin)", ".0f", False),
    tenor_panel("psi_pct", "Ψ  (% of one debt-service payment)", ".1f", False),
    tenor_panel("prob_loss", "P(V < 0)", ".0%", True),
    spacing=8,
).resolve_scale(x="shared", color="shared").properties(
    title=alt.TitleParams(
        "What the tenor is worth, and in which unit",
        subtitle=["Ψ is the actuarial quote and carries no annuity; Δr spreads it over the loan",
                  "The grey curve also changes which close years it contains"],
        anchor="start", fontSize=14))
```

Both curves fall, and the controlled one falls further. On the fixed cohort the margin-equivalent spread runs 242bp at a five-year tenor, 142bp at ten, 92bp at fifteen, 61bp at twenty and 44bp at twenty-five. The uncontrolled curve is flatter — 150bp to 44bp — and turns the wrong way in the bottom panel: $P(V_w<0)$ ticks up from 24% at $n=20$ to 29% at $n=25$, not because long tenors are riskier but because by then the only closes left in it are the 1985–1999 ones. Controlling the cohort strengthens the result rather than qualifying it, which is the reason to prefer it.

But the decline is not all mean reversion, and the middle panel says how much of it is. In the actuarial unit the fixed-cohort premium falls from 6.8% to 4.5% of a debt-service payment between $n=5$ and $n=25$ — about a third — while $\Delta r$ falls by four-fifths over the same range. The difference is the annuity: the same expected loss spread over more payments, accruing on a balance that takes longer to amortise. On the uncontrolled sample $\Psi$ barely moves at all, from 4.2% to 4.5%, so the whole of that curve's decline in $\Delta r$ is conversion rather than risk.

The claim that long tenors are cheap to cover therefore has two parts, and only one of them is about the real exchange rate. Reversion inside the window does genuine work — worth roughly a third of the premium between a five-year and a twenty-five-year horizon — and the loan's amortisation profile does the rest. The cleanest evidence for the first part is the bottom panel, where no annuity can enter: on the fixed cohort the share of windows ending in the red falls from 48% at $n=5$ to 29% at $n=25$. Time is what turns a coin toss into a one-in-three chance, and it is why this cover suits long-tenor project debt rather than working capital.

## Country groupings: what a cut of the pool can and cannot show {#sec-groupings}

Grouping cannot make the cover cheaper. Expectation is linear in the pool, so the pooled premium is a window-weighted average of its members and any partition of it averages back to the same number. What a grouping *can* show is two things: where the pooled price comes from, and whether the countries inside a group are one exposure or many — the second being the capital question rather than the price question. @fig-groups puts them side by side: the left panel prices the cover country by country within each group, the right reports the mean pairwise correlation of annual $\Delta\ln X$ inside it.

Two cuts, both on the 1985 pool. The first is the exchange-rate regime of the setup cell. The second is monetary history: countries split at a median annual inflation of 10% over 1985–2024, which separates twelve from thirty-eight. The two are not independent — all sixteen EUR-linked countries fall in the low-inflation group, so the regime cut is partly a proxy for the monetary one — and that overlap is itself worth seeing.

The sample choice matters here more than anywhere else in the paper. A 1995 start drops the 1994 CFA devaluation, which is the one episode that prices the EUR-linked group: on that sample the group costs 6bp against the floats' 44bp, and the peg reads as very nearly free cover. On the full sample it costs 49bp against 66bp. The regime result is not sample-robust in level, and stating it on the truncated sample would mean pricing CFA cover on a window that opens the year after the CFA devaluation.

```{python}
#| include: false
#| execution: {iopub.execute_input: '2026-09-17T07:26:31.046583Z', iopub.status.busy: '2026-09-17T07:26:31.045543Z', iopub.status.idle: '2026-09-17T07:26:31.086210Z', shell.execute_reply: '2026-09-17T07:26:31.085203Z'}
# Country groupings (@fig-groups): two cuts of the same 1985 pool, each reported
# on both sides of the only question a grouping can answer.
#   price   - the group's pooled premium, and the dispersion of its members
#   capital - the mean pairwise correlation of annual d ln X within the group,
#             i.e. whether the group is one exposure wearing several names
# Expectation is linear in the pool, so a grouping can neither create nor
# destroy premium (@sec-variation); it can only show where the pooled number
# comes from, and how much of the group's risk is common.
#
# The cuts are run on the 1985 pool deliberately. A 1995 start drops the 1994
# CFA devaluation, which is the one episode that prices the EUR-linked group,
# and the regime cut then reads as though the peg were nearly free.
median_inflation = (df.dropna(subset=["cpi"]).sort_values(["iso3", "year"])
                      .groupby("iso3")["cpi"]
                      .apply(lambda s: float(np.exp(np.median(np.diff(np.log(s.to_numpy())))) - 1)))

group_countries = pool_by_country.copy()
group_countries["regime"] = group_countries["iso3"].map(fx_regime).fillna("Flexible")
group_countries["median_inflation"] = group_countries["iso3"].map(median_inflation)
group_countries["inflation_group"] = np.where(
    group_countries["median_inflation"] >= 0.10, "Inflation >= 10%", "Inflation < 10%")

# Pairwise correlations of annual d ln X over the pool sample. min_periods keeps
# the short series out; .dropna() would empty the frame, as country coverage differs.
_x_wide = df[df["year"] >= pool_start_year].pivot(index="year", columns="iso3", values="X")
dlnx_corr = np.log(_x_wide).diff().corr(min_periods=10)


def mean_within_corr(iso_list):
    """Mean of the upper triangle of the within-group correlation matrix."""
    members = [c for c in iso_list if c in dlnx_corr.columns]
    if len(members) < 2:
        return np.nan
    sub = dlnx_corr.loc[members, members]
    return float(sub.where(np.triu(np.ones(sub.shape, dtype=bool), k=1)).stack().mean())


group_rows = []
for scheme, col in [("Exchange-rate regime", "regime"), ("Monetary history", "inflation_group")]:
    for name, members in group_countries.groupby(col):
        res = pool_res[pool_res["iso3"].isin(members["iso3"])]
        psi_g = -res["loss"].mean()
        group_rows.append({
            "scheme": scheme,
            "group": name,
            "n_countries": len(members),
            "n_windows": len(res),
            "pooled_dr_bp": 1e4 * (equivalent_rate(psi_g, discount_rate=discount_rate,
                                                   years=window_length) - discount_rate),
            "prob_loss": (res["V"] < 0).mean(),
            "median_dr_bp": 1e4 * members["rate_increase"].median(),
            "max_dr_bp": 1e4 * members["rate_increase"].max(),
            "worst": members.loc[members["rate_increase"].idxmax(), "country"],
            "n_zero": int((members["psi"] == 0).sum()),
            "mean_corr": mean_within_corr(members["iso3"].tolist()),
        })
groups = pd.DataFrame(group_rows)

# One row per country per scheme: the dots of the left panel.
group_points = pd.concat([
    group_countries.assign(scheme="Exchange-rate regime", group=group_countries["regime"]),
    group_countries.assign(scheme="Monetary history", group=group_countries["inflation_group"]),
], ignore_index=True)
group_points["dr_bp"] = 1e4 * group_points["rate_increase"]
# Seeded jitter: countries pile up at exactly zero and the strip is unreadable
# without it. Reproducible, and it only ever moves a dot off its own row's centre.
group_points["jitter"] = np.random.default_rng(0).uniform(-0.32, 0.32, len(group_points))

print(groups.to_string(index=False, formatters={
    "pooled_dr_bp": "{:.0f}bp".format, "median_dr_bp": "{:.0f}bp".format,
    "max_dr_bp": "{:.0f}bp".format, "prob_loss": "{:.0%}".format,
    "mean_corr": "{:+.2f}".format}))
print(f"\nAll Africa: pooled {dr_pool * 1e4:.0f}bp, median country "
      f"{pool_by_country['rate_increase'].median() * 1e4:.0f}bp, "
      f"mean pairwise correlation {mean_within_corr(pool_by_country['iso3'].tolist()):+.2f}")
print("\nregime against inflation group:")
print(pd.crosstab(group_countries["regime"], group_countries["inflation_group"]).to_string())
```

Right: mean pairwise correlation of annual $\Delta \ln X$ within the group - the capital side of the same cut.'

Regime does not separate the typical country. The median EUR-linked country prices at 43bp and the median float at 42bp — the same number — and their interquartile ranges, 11–83bp and 7–90bp, overlap almost completely. What the peg changes is the tail and the correlation. No EUR-linked country prices above 91bp (Gabon), while the floats run out to 189bp (the Democratic Republic of Congo) and 274bp (Libya); and the mean pairwise correlation within the CFA bloc is $+0.84$, against $+0.15$ among the floats. A book of sixteen CFA exposures is close to one exposure held sixteen times, because they share an anchor: it prices like a diversified book and behaves like a concentrated one. That is a capital finding rather than a pricing one, and it cuts against the group whose price looks safest.

ZAR-linked is two countries and twenty-eight windows once Lesotho is excluded for its CPI breaks, and its correlation of $+1.00$ is a single pair. It is drawn faded for that reason and should not be read as a regime result: it is the rand, observed twice.

Monetary history separates what the regime does not. The twelve high-inflation countries price at a pooled 70bp against 55bp for the other thirty-eight, and — unlike the regime cut — the gap sits in the middle of the distribution rather than in the tail: a median of 65bp against 36bp. They are also the least correlated group in the figure, at $+0.07$ against $+0.37$ for the low-inflation countries, and that $+0.37$ is itself inflated by the CFA bloc sitting inside it. The expensive group is the diversifiable one, which is the most useful combination a facility can be handed: the countries that most need the cover are the ones a pooled book can most afford to hold together.

Against the all-Africa pooled 58bp, then, a single price is a cross-subsidy running from the low-inflation countries to the high-inflation ones, while the CFA bloc pays roughly its own way and contributes most of the correlation. That is the tiering question of the previous section in a second guise, and it points the same way.

::: {.content-hidden}

## Outstanding robustness checks

The numbers above are a single point estimate from one sample, one tenor and one definition of indexation. The following checks are outstanding; each is a small extension of the machinery already in this document.

- **Sampling error on $\Psi$.** The 1,055 windows are heavily overlapping — a country with an unbroken series contributes 25 windows drawn from 40 annual observations — so a naive standard error is badly understated. *How:* country-block bootstrap: resample the 50 countries with replacement, recompute $\Psi$ and $\Delta r$ on each draw (10,000 draws), report the 5th–95th percentile band. A stationary block bootstrap over close years within country gives the complementary time-dimension band. @fig-bootstrap already does the country-block version on the 1995 pool; it needs extending to this sample and to $\Delta r$.
- **The cyclicality period of the real exchange rate.** The affordability result rests on the real rate mean-reverting inside a 15-year tenor — the decomposition above shows the $Q$-priced cover is a near-fair bet, which is only true if it reverts. The length of that cycle is asserted rather than estimated. *How:* fit an AR(1) on $\ln Q$ country by country and as a pooled panel with country fixed effects (bias-correct the pooled estimate), report the implied half-lives and set them against $n$. Complement with a panel unit-root test (Im–Pesaran–Shin): $\ln Q$ following a random walk is the null under which no facility of this kind is priceable.
- **Delayed inflation adjustment.** The project is assumed to reprice with $P_{i,t}$ contemporaneously. Real PPAs reset annually, off a lagged index, and often with a cap. *How:* replace $X_{i,t}$ by $P_{i,t-k}/S_{i,t}$ for $k \in \{0.25, 0.5, 1\}$ years, and by a capped variant in which the tariff rises by $\min(\pi_{i,t}, \bar{\pi})$, then re-price. The lag bites hardest exactly where the premium is largest — in the high-inflation tail — so this is the sensitivity most likely to move the headline. @sec-indexation makes the point qualitatively; this turns it into the same $\Delta r$ units.
- **Sample period.** Partly done: @fig-country-spread reprices every country on starts of 1985, 1990 and 1995, and the pooled premium falls 58bp, 55bp, 30bp across them — the 1995 start of @sec-results excludes the 1994 CFA devaluation. *How, for the rest:* add a 2000 start and report $N$, $\Psi$, $P(V_w<0)$ and $\Delta r$ as a table, and attribute the drop to episodes rather than to years by dropping the 1994-95 close cohort from the 1985 sample instead of truncating it.
- **Window length.** Done: @sec-tenor prices the cover at tenors from 5 to 25 years on this sample, holding the close cohort fixed so that the horizon is the only thing that varies. The premium does fall in $n$, but only about a third of the fall is mean reversion; the rest is the annuity conversion into $\Delta r$.
- **Country groupings.** Done: @sec-groupings cuts this pool by exchange-rate regime and by monetary history, reporting each group on the price side and the correlation side. @sec-variation runs the regime cut on the 1995 pool and still needs reconciling with it. A commodity-exporter split remains the natural third cut.
- **Correlation across countries and groups.** Diversification is the capital argument, and it depends on how much of the risk is common. *How:* the matrix of pairwise correlations of annual $\Delta \ln X$, ordered by regime, with mean within- and across-regime correlations (@fig-corr-heatmap, again on the other sample). The CFA bloc, moving against a common EUR anchor, is the obvious concentration; a single-factor decomposition — the share of variance taken by the first principal component — turns this into the number that sizes the capital.
- **Understanding the intertemporal hedge.** The result rests on two mechanisms that the exhibits above conflate, and separating them is the strongest check available. *How:* (i) *within-window reversion* — split each window's $V_w$ into its drawing phase and its repayment phase, and report what fraction of gross drawings is recovered by maturity among windows that end positive; (ii) *premium banking across windows* — 74% of windows never pay out at all, so the Facility accumulates premium against the ones that do. Simulate its running balance over a rolling cohort of vintages (say five new projects a year for twenty years) to show how long it takes to fund the first tail loss out of premium income, and how sensitive that is to the correlation structure above. Together these say whether the price is doing genuine intertemporal work or is merely the mean of a heavy-tailed variable.
