# Why the standard fixes overcharge: hedging is an inflation bet {#sec-hedging}

Refinancing into local currency and rolling NDF hedges are the same trade: covered interest parity pins the forward rate to the interest differential, $F = S_0(1+i_{LCU})/(1+i_{USD})$, by arbitrage. Both therefore charge the *full* differential

$$ i_{LCU} - i_{USD} \;=\; \underbrace{\mathbb{E}\big[\pi - \pi^{\$}\big]}_{\text{inflation diff.}} \;+\; \underbrace{\mathbb{E}\big[-\dot q\big]}_{\text{real depr.}} \;+\; \underbrace{rp}_{\text{risk premium}} $$

to shed an exposure of which the project — with indexed revenues — only ever bore the residual $-\dot x$.

## The parity accounting

Measured in units of the project's own (CPI-indexed) revenue, the extra cost of the local-currency loan over the USD loan collapses to $rp$ *if expectations are realised*: the inflation component is a wash in present value, paid as a certain coupon against an uncertain erosion of the nominal liability - which is the asymmetry @sec-nga-refi makes concrete. TODO: appendix derivation (see @sec-appendix).

## The hedger's residual risk position: long local inflation

The refinanced borrower's cash-flow health is $P_{i,t}/P_{i,0}$ against a liability fixed in local currency. Only realised inflation pays back the prepaid differential; realised *real* depreciation pays them nothing in cash — it merely vindicates the hedge counterfactually. The hedge therefore does not remove risk, it **rotates** it: a currency exposure becomes a forced long position in local inflation, whose losing branch is a stable, low-inflation currency (the Kenya path, @sec-kenya-refi).

That position cannot be structured away by choosing a different repayment profile. A *level* local-currency annuity is a fixed nominal payment against revenue growing with CPI, so coverage is weakest at the start; a schedule *escalating* at the UIP-implied depreciation rate matches payments to expected revenue growth and restores coverage in every year. But the two are the same bet under different weightings. Escalation settles a larger share of the liability at exchange rates further in the future, so the dispersion of the borrower's realised USD cost *widens*: @sec-nga-refi computes both on the realised Nigerian and Kenyan paths and finds that escalation removes every DSCR breach while increasing the spread between the best and worst outcome by about a tenth. Repayment structuring relocates the exposure between coverage and cost; it does not reduce it.

The Facility client of @sec-instrument, by contrast, holds no inflation position at all: DSCR is one by construction on every path, the premium is the same on every path, upside on real appreciation is kept and downside on real depreciation is insured.

# The instrument: an emergency liquidity facility for the real residual {#sec-instrument}

Let the **Facility** $G$ provide emergency liquidity. Whenever $R_{w,t}<0$, $G$ advances $100\,|R_{w,t}|$ so the project can meet its 100 of debt service; whenever $R_{w,t}>0$, the project escrows the surplus in an interest-bearing USD account to repay $G$ at maturity $\bar{t}$. Equivalently, $G$ tops the project's coverage back up to $\text{DSCR}=1$ in every period. Netting advances against escrowed surpluses, $G$'s present-value payout is

$$
L_w \;=\; D\,(-V_w)^{+}, \qquad \mathbb{E}[L_w] \;=\; -\,D\,\mathbb{E}[V_w]\ \text{ (mean basis)} ,
$$

so $G$ is made whole with interest when $V_w\ge 0$ and absorbs $D\,|V_w|$ when $V_w<0$. Here $V_w$ is the **net cover balance**: the discounted lifetime P&L already normalised by $A_{n,\rho}$, so it reads as a fraction of the debt stock. The actuarially fair premium covers $\mathbb{E}[L_w]$, abstracting from solvency capital (@sec-solvency) and profit loadings.

**Cost relative to the debt stock, and the LLCR.** Since debt service is $n$ payments of 100, the amount borrowed is their present value,

$$
D \;=\; 100\,A_{n,\rho}, \qquad A_{n,\rho}=\sum_{k=1}^{n}(1+\rho)^{-k}=\frac{1-(1+\rho)^{-n}}{\rho} .
$$

The debt stock is the natural denominator, because the cover is in effect insurance on the loan-life coverage ratio. The present value of dollar CFADS over the loan life is $\sum_{t=\underline{t}+1}^{\bar{t}} 100\,(1+R_{w,t})(1+\rho)^{-(t-\underline{t})} = D\,(1 + V_w)$, so

$$
\text{LLCR}_w \;=\; \frac{\text{PV}_0\!\big(\text{CFADS}^{\$}\big)}{D} \;=\; 1 + V_w .
$$

The instrument draws exactly when $\text{LLCR}_w<1$ and tops it back to one. Its expected cost per dollar of debt is therefore the expected shortfall of the loan-life coverage ratio below unity:

$$
\frac{\mathbb{E}[L_w]}{D} \;=\; -\,\mathbb{E}[V_w] \;=\; \mathbb{E}\big[\,1-\text{LLCR}_w\,\big]
$$

(with the option-aware refinement $\mathbb{E}\big[(1-\text{LLCR}_w)^{+}\big]$ once the asymmetry of $L_w$ is priced).

**The three premium quotes (and the $A$-identity).** Multiplying by $A_{n,\rho}$ converts an annuity into a present value; dividing converts a present value into an annuity. The actuarially fair *level annual premium* is therefore

$$
\Psi \;=\; \frac{\mathbb{E}[L_w]}{A_{n,\rho}} \;=\; -\,100\,\mathbb{E}[V_w],
\qquad
\frac{\Psi}{100} \;=\; -\,\mathbb{E}[V_w] .
$$

So $-\mathbb{E}[V_w]$ is simultaneously the premium as a fraction of each **annual debt service payment** and — because $D = 100\,A_{n,\rho}$ — the expected PV loss as a fraction of the **debt stock**. One number, two readings: this is the $A$-identity, and it is the pivot between the actuarial and the credit quote.

Dividing by $A_{n,\rho}$ a second time gives

$$
\frac{\Psi}{D} \;=\; -\,\frac{\mathbb{E}[V_w]}{A_{n,\rho}} ,
$$

a flat annual payment expressed as a share of the *original principal*. **This is not the equivalent interest-rate spread, except on a bullet loan.** On an annuity-amortising loan a margin accrues on the declining outstanding balance — on average roughly 65% of the original principal — so the margin-equivalent add-on $\Delta r$ is about half again as large. It is computed exactly by `equivalent_rate()` in @sec-method, which treats the expected loss as additional principal and solves

$$
A_{n,\;\rho+\Delta r} \;=\; \frac{A_{n,\rho}}{1 + \big|\,\mathbb{E}[V_w]\,\big|} .
$$

We quote the premium to actuaries as a share of the covered exposure (debt service), and to investors as the margin-equivalent $\Delta r$.

# Data and method {#sec-method}

For every country and every rolling 15-year window since 1995, we compute the discounted sum of cumulative returns $R_{w,t} = X_{i,t}/X_{i,\underline{t}} - 1$ — the present value of the lifetime P&L, `V_raw` in the code — and normalise by the annuity factor $A_{n,\rho}$ into the net cover balance $V$, a PV per unit of debt stock, i.e. the expected LLCR shortfall of @sec-instrument. `compute_terminal_residuals_wdi`, defined in the hidden setup code at the top of the document, mirrors `source/data_analysis_functions.py::compute_terminal_residuals`, operating directly on the WDI data; `equivalent_rate` performs the amortising-loan margin conversion to $\Delta r$.

# Results: the cover costs basis points {#sec-results}

Pooled over all rolling 15-year windows (~668 windows, 50 countries, $\rho = 5\%$): expected loss $\approx$ 2.03% of debt stock in PV, with only ~16% of windows producing any loss. Quoted three ways: **~2.0% of each debt-service payment** (the actuarial quote), **~20bp of principal per year flat**, or **~30bp on the loan margin** of a 15-year annuity loan (20bp for a bullet).

# Two tariffs and a balance sheet between them {#sec-indexation}

Everything above assumes the project's dollar revenue tracks $X=P/S$ exactly, which is to say that the tariff is indexed continuously and contemporaneously to the domestic price level. That assumption does the central work --- it is what makes the inflation component drop out and leaves only the real residual as risk --- so it needs a sensitivity rather than a footnote. But the assumption has to be relaxed in the right place, because there are two tariffs here and they are different kinds of object.

The tariff a utility is **allowed to charge** its customers is a political variable. It is set by a regulator, revised on a cycle that slips, and frozen when the cost of living is salient. The tariff the utility has **contracted to pay** an IPP is not political. It is a contract, usually fully indexed, usually enforceable, and often standing behind a sovereign letter of support. The two do not have to move together, and when they do not, the difference lands on the offtaker's balance sheet. That balance sheet can carry the difference for a while. It cannot carry it indefinitely --- which is precisely what the financial condition of Africa's state utilities records.

So the model has three layers, and `compute_indexed_residuals` now takes each separately:

| Layer | What it is | Parameter |
|---|---|---|
| PPA tariff | what the IPP is contractually owed | `lag`, `reset_every`, `ref_window`, `threshold`, `share` |
| Retail tariff | what the offtaker is allowed to collect | `retail_rule` (same five knobs) |
| Offtaker balance sheet | absorbs the difference, up to a point | `buffer_capacity`, `buffer_passthrough` |

**Layer 1 is in good shape.** South Africa's REIPPPP PPAs are standardised, non-negotiable, rand-denominated, 20-year and fully CPI-indexed, with the bid tariff quoted at a Base Date in the RFP and escalated each 1 April by the preceding calendar year's CPI. Kenya's PPAs oblige Kenya Power to settle within 30 days, with National Treasury letters of support behind the obligation.

**Layer 2 is where the politics lives.** NERC owed seven biannual minor reviews from February 2016 and conducted none until 2019; the tariff that should have reached N51/kWh stayed at N31.8. Ghana suspended its adjustment formula and delayed cost-reflective increases through 2014--17. Kenya Power withdrew its 2026 tariff application citing inflation, with an election in view. Argentina held tariffs frozen from 2002 to 2015 across a currency collapse. Freezes cluster on devaluations, because that is when adjusting is most costly politically.

**Layer 3 is real, thin, and mostly fiscal.** Nigeria's eleven DisCos ran a N1.83trn market shortfall between 2015 and 2019. The GenCos were kept whole not by the DisCos but by the sovereign: N701bn of NBET payment-assurance covering 80--90% of generation and gas invoices for 2017--18, a further N600bn covering 100% for 2019--20, and N3.3trn agreed as final settlement of 2015--2025 liabilities. Where no sovereign stepped in, the IPP tier absorbed it directly --- Kenya Power paid KSh4.73bn against KSh21bn demanded by three IPPs over five months of 2023; ZESCO owes its four IPPs just under \$800m, one of them enforcing \$350m in the London High Court; Ghana's grid-connected IPPs have threatened shutdown over accumulated PPA arrears.

It is worth noticing what those payment-assurance facilities are. They are emergency liquidity, advanced to bridge exactly this gap, sized in the hundreds of billions of naira, and provided ad hoc and after the fact by a sovereign that had not priced the risk. The instrument this paper proposes is the ex-ante, priced version of something governments are already doing.

```{python}
#| label: tbl-indexation
#| tbl-cap: 'Layer 1: cost of the cover when the PPA''s own indexation departs from the ideal, with the offtaker assumed to pay in full. All rows are computed on the same monthly grid; see the note below on the annual-grid headline number.'
#| execution: {iopub.execute_input: '2026-09-17T07:26:35.957304Z', iopub.status.busy: '2026-09-17T07:26:35.957304Z', iopub.status.idle: '2026-09-17T07:26:40.336374Z', shell.execute_reply: '2026-09-17T07:26:40.336374Z'}
import sys
if '../source' not in sys.path:
    sys.path.insert(0, '../source')
import data_analysis_functions as daf

r_month = (1 + discount_rate) ** (1 / 12) - 1
af_15 = (1 - (1 + discount_rate) ** -window_length) / discount_rate


def premium_row(label, **kw):
    """Pooled premium under one rule, as a margin add-on in basis points."""
    res = daf.compute_indexed_residuals(
        df, years=window_length, discount_rate=discount_rate,
        start_year=start_year, steps_per_year=12, **kw)
    e_loss = -res['loss'].mean()
    return {'Rule': label,
            'E[loss] (% debt)': 100 * e_loss,
            'Margin add-on (bp)': 1e4 * e_loss / af_15,
            'P(loss) (%)': 100 * (res['loss'] < 0).mean(),
            '5th pct V/A (%)': 100 * res['net_pv_by_debt_stock'].quantile(0.05),
            'Windows': len(res)}


ppa_rules = [
    ('Full indexation (model assumption)',         dict()),
    ('Monthly reset, 1m lag',                      dict(lag=1, reset_every=1)),
    ('Quarterly reset, projected index',           dict(lag=0, reset_every=3)),
    ('REIPPPP: annual reset, 9m lag, 12m avg ref', dict(lag=9, reset_every=12, ref_window=12)),
    ('Biannual reset, 5% materiality trigger',     dict(lag=6, reset_every=6, threshold=np.log(1.05))),
    ('Materiality trigger, 25%',                   dict(lag=3, reset_every=1, threshold=np.log(1.25))),
    ('Partial indexation, 50% pass-through',       dict(lag=0, reset_every=1, share=0.5)),
]

ppa_sensitivity = pd.DataFrame([premium_row(name, **rule) for name, rule in ppa_rules])
ppa_sensitivity['vs full (bp)'] = (ppa_sensitivity['Margin add-on (bp)']
                                   - ppa_sensitivity['Margin add-on (bp)'].iloc[0])
print(ppa_sensitivity.to_string(index=False, float_format='%.2f'))

annual = daf.compute_indexed_residuals(
    df, years=window_length, discount_rate=discount_rate, start_year=start_year, steps_per_year=1)
annual_bp = 1e4 * -annual['loss'].mean() / af_15
monthly_bp = ppa_sensitivity['Margin add-on (bp)'].iloc[0]
print(f"\nAnnual grid, full indexation (the headline number): {annual_bp:.1f}bp over {len(annual)} windows.")
print(f"Monthly grid, full indexation: {monthly_bp:.1f}bp. The {abs(monthly_bp - annual_bp):.1f}bp "
      f"difference is the re-aggregation alone, not an indexation effect.")
```

Layer 1 is not where the risk is. Every rule that a PPA actually contains --- monthly reset, quarterly formula, REIPPPP's annual 1 April escalation off a nine-month-old twelve-month average, a biannual review with a 5% trigger --- moves the premium by between $-1.2$bp and $-0.1$bp against an 18.1bp baseline. This is the same conclusion the inflation-linked bond literature reaches about indexation lags: at tenors beyond a few years the lag choice has little consequence. A pure lag shifts *which* stretch of inflation the contract captures without changing *how much*, so in steady state it costs nothing and bites only when inflation accelerates.

What does cost money is indexation that is incomplete rather than late. A 25% materiality trigger takes the premium to 30.1bp; halving the pass-through takes it to 92.8bp, more than five times the baseline. So the paper's claim should be stated precisely: cheap cover requires a PPA that indexes *fully*, not one that indexes *promptly*. That is a condition the standardised African PPAs mostly satisfy.

One caveat on reading the table. Sub-annual rules require interpolating the annual series onto a monthly grid and averaging dollar revenue back up over the year, and that re-aggregation moves the full-indexation baseline from 19.6bp to 18.1bp on its own --- larger than every contractual-lag effect above. Read the differences within the table, not its levels, and do not quote 18.1bp as the paper's number.

```{python}
                               buffer_capacity=0.5, buffer_arrears_rate=r_month))
buffer_rows.append(premium_row('Retail 50% pass-through, buffer 1 yr',

                               buffer_arrears_rate=r_month))

offtaker_sensitivity = pd.DataFrame(buffer_rows)
offtaker_sensitivity['vs full (bp)'] = (offtaker_sensitivity['Margin add-on (bp)']
```

This is where the risk actually is, and the numbers are not close.

Give the offtaker an unlimited balance sheet and the retail tier is invisible: a 4.5-year freeze changes the premium by nothing at all, because the utility absorbs the whole wedge and the IPP is paid its indexed PPA tariff throughout. That row is today's model. It is the assumption that the offtaker always pays, stated explicitly for the first time.

Make the balance sheet finite and the channel dominates everything in @tbl-indexation. The same 4.5-year freeze costs $+10.7$bp with two years of absorption capacity, $+16.6$bp with one year, $+21.6$bp with six months, and $+25.2$bp with three. At half a year of capacity the premium roughly doubles, from 18.1bp to 39.8bp, and the fifth-percentile window falls from $-11.6\%$ to $-26.1\%$ of debt stock. Set against this, the largest PPA-tier timing effect in @tbl-indexation was 1.2bp, and it went the other way. **The offtaker channel is one to two orders of magnitude larger than the indexation channel.** What the instrument is really covering is not lag in the PPA; it is the offtaker's inability to carry a political wedge.

The sovereign backstop is decisive, and this is the row that matters for design. Routing 85% of the un-absorbed deficit to a payment-assurance facility --- the share NBET actually covered of Nigerian generation invoices in 2017--18 --- takes a six-month-buffer freeze from $+21.6$bp back to $+1.9$bp. Almost the entire cost of the offtaker channel is the *absence* of a backstop rather than the freeze itself. That is the same finding as the true-up result in a different guise, and it points the same way: the cheap intervention is not a better indexation clause, it is a committed liquidity line sitting behind the offtaker.

Two honest limits. Buffer capacity is the parameter with the least direct evidence behind it: Nigeria's N1.83trn shortfall over five years and Kenya Power's settlement of a fifth of IPP invoices over five months in 2023 bracket the plausible range but do not pin it, and the premium is roughly linear in it over the range shown, so the number matters. And the analysis stops at a capacity of three months, because below that the squeeze reaches the IPP inside the first year and is absorbed into the DSCR $=1$ calibration at financial close, which mechanically shrinks the contract and makes the premium fall again --- an artifact of the normalisation, not a finding.

```{python}
#| label: tbl-tariff-evidence
#| tbl-cap: 'Layer 2 in the data: does the retail tariff keep up? Doing Business price of electricity (US cents/kWh for a standardised consumer, DB16-20 methodology) merged to the WDI panel, 2014-19.'
#| execution: {iopub.execute_input: '2026-09-17T07:26:49.328918Z', iopub.status.busy: '2026-09-17T07:26:49.328918Z', iopub.status.idle: '2026-09-17T07:26:51.067773Z', shell.execute_reply: '2026-09-17T07:26:51.067773Z'}
import statsmodels.api as sm

tariff = pd.read_csv('../data/db_electricity_price.csv')
ev = (tariff.merge(df[['iso3', 'year', 'exchange_rate', 'cpi', 'X']], on=['iso3', 'year'])
            .sort_values(['iso3', 'year']))
grp = ev.groupby('iso3')
for col, new in [('us_cents_per_kwh', 'd_usd'), ('X', 'd_X'),
                 ('exchange_rate', 'd_s'), ('cpi', 'd_p')]:
    ev[new] = grp[col].transform(lambda s: np.log(s).diff())
ev = ev.dropna(subset=['d_usd', 'd_X']).copy()
ev['d_lcu'] = ev['d_usd'] + ev['d_s']              # nominal retail tariff in LCU
ev['wedge'] = ev['d_usd'] - ev['d_X']              # realised minus fully-indexed

def _ols(y, xs, label, data=ev):
    fit = sm.OLS(data[y], sm.add_constant(data[xs])).fit(
        cov_type='cluster', cov_kwds={'groups': data['iso3']})
    terms = '  '.join(f'{k}={fit.params[k]:+.2f} ({fit.bse[k]:.2f})' for k in ['const'] + xs)
    print(f'  {label:38s} {terms}   n={int(fit.nobs)}  R2={fit.rsquared:.2f}')

print(f'{ev["iso3"].nunique()} countries, {len(ev)} country-year changes, '
      f'{int(ev["year"].min())}-{int(ev["year"].max())}\n')
print('Does the nominal retail tariff track domestic prices?')
_ols('d_lcu', ['d_p'], 'd ln(LCU tariff) on d ln CPI')

print('\nAnd how does it behave in the states that stress the balance sheet?')
_ols('d_usd', ['d_s'], 'd ln(USD tariff) on depreciation')
_ols('wedge', ['d_s'], 'wedge on depreciation')
_ols('wedge', ['d_s'], '  excl. |inflation| > 25%', ev[ev['d_p'].abs() < 0.25])
for label, dummies in [('country fixed effects', 'iso3'), ('year fixed effects', 'year')]:
    X = pd.concat([ev[['d_s']], pd.get_dummies(ev[dummies], prefix='fe', drop_first=True).astype(float)], axis=1)
    fit = sm.OLS(ev['wedge'], X).fit(cov_type='cluster', cov_kwds={'groups': ev['iso3']})
    print(f"  {'  with ' + label:38s} d_s={fit.params['d_s']:+.2f} ({fit.bse['d_s']:.2f})"
          f"                    n={int(fit.nobs)}")

big, calm = ev[ev['d_s'] > 0.10], ev[ev['d_s'] <= 0.10]
print(f'\n  median wedge, years with >10% depreciation (n={len(big)}): {big["wedge"].median():+.3f}')
print(f'  median wedge, all other years         (n={len(calm)}): {calm["wedge"].median():+.3f}')
```

Read in the two-tier frame, @tbl-tariff-evidence is about layer 2 --- what consumers actually pay, and therefore how much stress the balance sheet is under. It is not a test of whether the IPP's PPA is indexed, and the earlier draft of this section made that mistake.

On average, the news for the buffer is better than the anecdotes suggest. Nominal retail tariffs track CPI close to one-for-one ($\beta = 0.98$, s.e. $0.21$), and in the states that matter they do better than full CPI indexation, not worse: the USD price of electricity is statistically indistinguishable from *invariant* to the exchange rate ($+0.12$, s.e. $0.10$), and the wedge against a fully-indexed tariff rises with depreciation at $+0.62$, strengthening to $+0.93$ once hyperinflation episodes are excluded and surviving country and year fixed effects. In years with more than 10% depreciation the median country's retail tariff does about 13 log points better than pure CPI indexation would deliver; in calm years it does about 6 points worse. That is what Ghana's AAF, MYTO's indices and Kenya's forex charge are built to do --- they index to the exchange rate, not only to the price level, precisely because the costs being recovered are dollar PPA obligations.

So the typical year does not stress the buffer much. What erodes it is the roughly $-2\%$ per year of real drift, which shows up as quasi-fiscal deficit rather than as any single event, and what breaks it is the discrete political freeze. Freezes are country-episodes --- Nigeria 2016--19, Argentina 2002--15 --- not an average slope, and a panel of five annual differences per country cannot see them. They are exactly what @tbl-offtaker prices, and the case for the instrument rests on them rather than on the average.

Three reasons not to lean hard on the regressions. The sample is five differences per country over 2014--19 on a standardised-consumer methodology. Doing Business converts to USD at its own reference rate while $X$ uses the WDI annual average, so a systematic conversion-date offset would generate a wedge correlated with depreciation --- though the near-zero loading of the USD price on the exchange rate is hard to reconcile with a pure timing artefact, which would show up near $-1$. And 2014--19 spans the oil price collapse, which pushes fuel-charge components down and plausibly explains the negative drift in calm years. Pinning layer 2 down properly needs a panel of local-currency tariff schedules with adjustment dates, and pinning layer 3 down needs utility payables; both are the natural next piece of data work.

# Country variation, regimes, and diversification {#sec-variation}

Expected loss ranges from exactly zero (Kenya: no window since 1995 ends PV-net below its start) to ~111bp of principal per year (Nigeria, where every losing window straddles the 1999 unification). Countries are classified into three exchange-rate regime groups (IMF AREAER, predominant arrangement 2000-2023): EUR-linked (CFA zone + Comoros, Cape Verde), ZAR-linked (CMA), and Flexible.

```{python}
# Ported from consolidated_currency_analysis.ipynb, cell 18.
# Mean pairwise correlation statistics
def mean_pairwise_corr(corr_matrix, group):
    sub = corr_matrix.loc[group, group]
    mask = np.triu(np.ones(sub.shape, dtype=bool), k=1)
    vals = sub.where(mask).stack()
    return vals.mean(), vals.std(), len(vals)

def mean_cross_corr(corr_matrix, g1, g2):
    vals = corr_matrix.loc[g1, g2].stack()
    return vals.mean(), vals.std(), len(vals)
```

```{python}
# Ported from consolidated_currency_analysis.ipynb, cell 20.
# Bootstrap confidence intervals (country-block resampling, 10,000 draws)
def bootstrap_premium(res_df, n_boot=10000, seed=42):
    rng = np.random.default_rng(seed)
    countries = res_df['country'].unique()
    n = len(countries)
    country_losses = {c: res_df.loc[res_df['country'] == c, 'loss'].values for c in countries}
    boot = np.empty(n_boot)
    for b in range(n_boot):
        sampled = rng.choice(countries, size=n, replace=True)
        all_losses = np.concatenate([country_losses[c] for c in sampled])
        boot[b] = all_losses.mean()
    point = res_df['loss'].mean()
    return {'point': point, 'se': boot.std(),
            'ci_lo': np.percentile(boot, 2.5), 'ci_hi': np.percentile(boot, 97.5),
            'distribution': boot}

# Run bootstrap for overall and per-regime

for regime in ['EUR-linked', 'ZAR-linked', 'Flexible']:
    boot_results[regime] = bootstrap_premium(residuals[residuals['regime'] == regime])

# Print summary

print("=" * 70)
for group, b in boot_results.items():
    print(f"{group:>12}: premium = {b['point']*100:.3f}%  "
          f"SE = {b['se']*100:.3f}%  "
          f"95% CI = [{b['ci_lo']*100:.3f}%, {b['ci_hi']*100:.3f}%]")

# Pre-bin bootstrap distributions in pandas to avoid Altair's 5000-row limit
group_order = ['All', 'EUR-linked', 'ZAR-linked', 'Flexible']
group_colors = ['steelblue', '#4c78a8', '#f58518', '#54a24b']

binned_rows = []
annot_rows = []
for group, b in boot_results.items():

    counts, edges = np.histogram(dist, bins=50)
    centers = (edges[:-1] + edges[1:]) / 2
    for c, cnt in zip(centers, counts):
```

# Worked examples: how the cover pans out for an investor {#sec-examples}

At financial close, sponsors commonly plan to refinance their hard-currency exposure quickly. The examples below run the actual data through three structures - naked USD debt, USD debt + facility, and a local-currency refinance at close - for the paths investors fear (Nigeria 2014) and the paths where the hedge is pure cost (Kenya 2009). All ledgers are in USD, discounted at the USD rate (5%), against the baseline of the original USD loan (principal 772, flat debt service 100/yr over 10 years).

## Nigeria 2014: the path the refinance-minded investor fears {#sec-nga-ledger}


## Nigeria 2014, refinanced: the bet, not the bill {#sec-nga-refi}

The honest counterfactual first. Converting every naira payment back to USD at realised rates, the naira loan is ex-post *cheaper* than the USD loan in present value (~524 against 772): depreciation outran the differential the coupon priced. So the case against the refinance is **not** that it costs more in expectation — a competent counterparty can falsify that on Nigeria's own decade. The case is that it swaps a contingent, insurable exposure for an uninsured directional position on inflation.

Two facts make that concrete.

**The level naira annuity breaches DSCR immediately** (0.77 in 2015, 0.89 in 2016) — and the breach is not a devaluation effect. Once the loan is in naira, the exchange rate is irrelevant to coverage: revenue and debt service are both in naira. Nigerian CPI inflation in 2015 was 9.0%, and $1.090 \times 100 / 142.3 = 0.77$. The project defaults in year one on a path where the hedge turned out to be *ex-post correct*.

**That breach is fixable by escalating the schedule** at the UIP-implied 8% — and fixing it makes the inflation position larger, not smaller. Both schedules price the same loan at the same coupon and have identical present value at close; they differ only in when the liability is settled, and therefore in how much of it is converted at exchange rates that have not happened yet.

```{python}
#| label: tbl-nga-refi
#| tbl-cap: 'The 2014 naira refinance (13% coupon): USD-converted payments and DSCR against indexed revenues.'
#| execution: {iopub.execute_input: '2026-09-17T07:26:57.221555Z', iopub.status.busy: '2026-09-17T07:26:57.221555Z', iopub.status.idle: '2026-09-17T07:26:57.235505Z', shell.execute_reply: '2026-09-17T07:26:57.234916Z'}
# New (session 2026-08-31): naira refinance at close, 10y annuity at 13%.
r_ngn, T_ref = 0.13, 10
af_usd10 = (1 - 1.05 ** -T_ref) / 0.05
af_ngn10 = (1 - (1 + r_ngn) ** -T_ref) / r_ngn
D_usd = 100 * af_usd10                       # 772.2
pay_ngn = D_usd * S0 / af_ngn10              # fixed naira annuity
CPI0 = win.cpi.iloc[0]
refi = pd.DataFrame({
    'year': win.year.iloc[1:].astype(int).values,
    'pay_usd': (pay_ngn / win.exchange_rate.iloc[1:]).values,
    'rev_ngn': (100 * S0 * win.cpi.iloc[1:] / CPI0).values,
})
refi['dscr_ngn'] = refi.rev_ngn / pay_ngn
pv_refi = float(np.sum(refi.pay_usd.values * 1.05 ** -np.arange(1, T_ref + 1)))
print(f"Naira annuity: N{pay_ngn:,.0f}/yr = {pay_ngn / S0:.1f} USD at close FX (vs 100 for the USD loan)")
print(f"PV of USD-converted naira payments @5%: {pv_refi:.1f}  vs USD loan {D_usd:.1f}")
refi.round(2)
```

```{python}
#| label: tbl-schedule-bet
#| tbl-cap: Level vs escalating local-currency schedules on the realised Nigerian and Kenyan paths. Escalation removes the DSCR breaches and simultaneously widens the dispersion of realised USD cost.
#| execution: {iopub.execute_input: '2026-09-17T07:26:57.240062Z', iopub.status.busy: '2026-09-17T07:26:57.238989Z', iopub.status.idle: '2026-09-17T07:26:57.260952Z', shell.execute_reply: '2026-09-17T07:26:57.260952Z'}
# Repayment structuring relocates the exposure between coverage and cost.
# The escalator is set at the UIP-implied expected depreciation (coupon - USD rate),
# so both schedules price the same loan and have identical PV at the coupon.
sched_rows = []
for iso_s, y0_s, coupon_s, lab_s in [('NGA', 2014, 0.13, 'Nigeria 2014'), ('KEN', 2009, 0.12, 'Kenya 2009')]:
    esc_s = coupon_s - 0.05
    ws = df[(df.iso3 == iso_s) & (df.year >= y0_s) & (df.year <= y0_s + 10)].sort_values('year').reset_index(drop=True)
    S0_s, CPI0_s = ws.exchange_rate.iloc[0], ws.cpi.iloc[0]
    tt = np.arange(1, 11)
    level_s = np.full(10, D_usd * S0_s / ((1 - (1 + coupon_s) ** -10) / coupon_s))
    escal_s = (D_usd * S0_s / np.sum((1 + esc_s) ** (tt - 1) / (1 + coupon_s) ** tt)) * (1 + esc_s) ** (tt - 1)
    rev_s = 100 * S0_s * (ws.cpi.iloc[1:].values / CPI0_s)     # indexed local-currency revenue
    fx_s = ws.exchange_rate.iloc[1:].values
    for name_s, pay_s in [('level', level_s), ('escalating', escal_s)]:
        dscr_s = rev_s / pay_s
        sched_rows.append({'case': lab_s, 'schedule': name_s,
                           'min DSCR': dscr_s.min(), 'yrs < 1.0': int((dscr_s < 1).sum()),
                           'USD PV': float(np.sum(pay_s / fx_s * 1.05 ** -tt))})
sched = pd.DataFrame(sched_rows)
spread = (sched.query("case=='Kenya 2009'").set_index('schedule')['USD PV']
          - sched.query("case=='Nigeria 2014'").set_index('schedule')['USD PV'])
print(f"USD loan PV {D_usd:.1f}; the facility holds the same debt at DSCR = 1 on every path.")
print(f"Best-to-worst spread in realised USD cost: level {spread['level']:.1f}, "
      f"escalating {spread['escalating']:.1f}  ({spread['escalating'] / spread['level'] - 1:+.1%})")
sched.round({'min DSCR': 2, 'USD PV': 1})
```

## Kenya 2009: the certain coupon with no offset {#sec-kenya-refi}

The shilling refinance pays a ~7-point differential against realised depreciation of ~2.7%/yr: every single USD-converted payment exceeds the USD loan's 100, an ex-post overpayment of ~200bp of principal per year for a decade — while $X$ never PV-net fell below any window start since 1995, so the Facility client paid ~20bp and never drew.

## Scenario matrix

| | Certain annual cost | Nigeria 2014 path | Kenya 2009 path | Failure mode |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| USD debt, naked | 0 | technical default 2015-17 and 2023-24 | fine | real depreciation |
| **USD debt + facility** | **20bp pooled / ~111bp standalone (Nigeria)** | every shortfall bridged, no default | premium paid, never drawn | none on any sample path |
| Refinance to LCU, level | full differential (contractual) | ex-post cheap in PV, **but DSCR breach yrs 1-2** | ex-post ~200bp/yr overpaid | long inflation; coverage fails if inflation undershoots |
| Refinance to LCU, escalating | full differential (contractual) | no DSCR breach; ex-post cheapest of the four | **worst of the four ex post** | long inflation, amplified; negative amortisation, market depth |
| Rolling NDF hedge | differential, repriced each roll | forward points explode after each deval | overpays like the refinance | rollover at the worst moment |

# Solvency: what capital the insurer actually needs {#sec-solvency}

Two distinct commitments. The *liquidity* commitment is bounded by one year of covered debt service: since $X > 0$, the Facility can never advance more than one year's debt service in any year (worst observed single-year shortfall: ~75%, Nigeria 2024) — cheap for a AAA balance sheet such as the AfDB's to stand behind. The *solvency* capital must instead be sized off the terminal-loss tail of the (diversified) covered book, i.e. the upper tail of $L_w = D\,(-V_w)^{+}$ (equivalently the left tail of $V_w$).

# Policy design and conclusion {#sec-policy}

About 30bp pooled - but adverse selection (the Nigerias buy, the Kenyas don't) unravels pooled pricing toward Nigeria's ~165bp standalone, arguing for embedding the cover in DFI lending terms or tiering premia by country (@fig-rate-by-country).

**Positioning in the current landscape.** The instrument is the complement, not the competitor, of the local-currency agenda: TCX and the Persaud partial FX guarantee operate on the *nominal* rate for lenders who convert; EcoInvest Brasil's FX liquidity line and this facility operate on *liquidity against the real component* for debt that stays in hard currency. The emerging hybrid PPA frameworks (Kenya, Nov 2025 / Jan 2026 regulations) explicitly retain a hard-currency component for international debt service - exactly the slice this facility makes safe. ## The wrong decomposition and the right one

The market treats this exposure as *nominal* FX risk. But nominal depreciation decomposes as

$$
\dot s_{i,t} \;=\; \underbrace{\big(\pi_{i,t} - \pi^{\$}_{t}\big)}_{\text{inflation differential}} \;+\; \underbrace{\big(-\dot q_{i,t}\big)}_{\text{real depreciation}} ,
$$

and an inflation-indexed tariff passes the inflation component straight through to revenues. Because $X=P/S$, taking logs and differencing gives the annual identity $\dot x_{i,t} = \pi_{i,t} - \dot s_{i,t}$ — inflation net of nominal depreciation, which is real appreciation $\dot q_{i,t}$ plus US inflation $\pi^{\$}_{t}$. Cumulating the annual observations from close,

$$
\ln\!\big(1+R_{w,t}\big) \;=\; x_{i,t}-x_{i,\underline{t}} \;=\; \sum_{u=\underline{t}+1}^{t}\big(\pi_{i,u}-\dot s_{i,u}\big) .
$$

The per-period P&L is thus the cumulative growth of $X$ since financial close. The project gains exactly when domestic inflation has cumulatively outpaced nominal depreciation, and falls into shortfall when the currency has depreciated *in real terms*. The inflation level itself drops out — it is passed through by the indexed tariff — leaving only the real component as risk. @sec-hedging shows what it costs to ignore this; the instrument of @sec-instrument prices only the residual.
